lessons.title: 3.1.1 Language of Page
lessons.objective: Identify the default human language in markup

content.text: Learning objectives
Identify the default human language in markup. This lesson addresses WCAG 2.2 3.1.1 Language of Page (Level A).
Why this matters

Screen readers use language information to select pronunciation rules and voices. A page in Filipino announced with an English voice can make familiar words difficult to recognize. The default language describes the human language of the main content, not the programming language or a visitor’s identity.
How to apply the criterion

Set the language on the root html element, for example <html lang="en"> for an English page. Choose a valid language tag appropriate to the actual content; setting the same tag on every site regardless of language defeats its purpose. Pages with several languages still need an appropriate default for the page.
Real-world example

A bilingual course home page is mostly written in English, but its HTML has no language setting. Speech output may use a voice selected for an unrelated language. Put lang="en" on the root element, then mark any applicable language changes on the passages themselves. The page language is the predominant language, not necessarily the language of every word.
Welcome

A server-side template should set the value for every localized page, including error pages. Inspect the final rendered HTML after localization; a translation service that changes the text but leaves lang="en" on a Filipino page introduces a mismatch. The attribute identifies a language; it does not translate content or ensure that a particular voice is installed.
Review and testing

A browser setting and an HTML lang attribute serve different purposes. Inspect the page source and the accessibility tree, then test text using a screen reader with automatic language switching. If the page is mostly Filipino, use an appropriate Filipino language tag rather than assuming English.
Checking a multilingual page

A language tag should describe the language of the document, including templates generated after a visitor changes the interface language. Check both initial server output and the final DOM after a client-side language switch. The title, navigation, form messages and main text may not all be translated at once. If one translation is incomplete, decide which language predominates and mark applicable passages in another language separately.

A valid tag such as en, fil or fr conveys language, while a regional subtag can add detail when useful. Inventing a tag or using a country flag as the only indicator does not supply equivalent machine-readable information. Testing should include a browser inspector and, when available, a screen reader configured to change voices by language. Voice availability varies, so inspect the markup as well as listening.
Inheritance and page templates

The language on the root element is inherited by its descendants unless a more specific language is set. In a multi-page application, check the root element generated for each page rather than only the shared template. In a single-page application, changing visible content to another primary language may require updating the document language as part of that transition. A regional tag can add useful detail, but only if it accurately describes the content.

A common failure occurs when a translated page changes its words while retaining the original template’s language. Compare the text and root attribute after navigating between translations, including after a reload. Automated checks can detect a missing or invalid tag, but a person must still determine whether the tag describes the actual language.
Walkthrough: auditing translated pages

Imagine a course catalogue with English and Filipino versions. Open the English page, inspect its root html element, and record the language tag. Follow the link to the Filipino version and inspect the root again. The text may change while the application shell remains mounted; if the root still says English, a screen reader that uses language information may apply an inappropriate pronunciation. Update the document language when the route changes, and ensure that a direct link and browser refresh produce the same correct result.

Next inspect the language selector itself. A control named “English” or “Filipino” identifies the choice, but that label does not establish the language of the destination document. Use a valid language tag representing the main language, and review any embedded passages that differ under the separate language-of-parts requirement. An automated rule that finds an attribute cannot determine whether the selected language matches the text; compare it with the content and listen when suitable speech voices are available.

If the page contains equally substantial sections in multiple languages, decide which language best describes the document as a whole and explicitly identify relevant changes in its parts. Record the content examined, the actual attribute, and whether navigation changed it. This makes the outcome reproducible and reveals errors that appear only after a client-side transition.
Apply the distinction

Consider a localized single-page application where the navigation stays in English but the main article changes to Spanish. The default language should reflect the predominant content of the current page; identify the English navigation separately if appropriate. A hard-coded English root can remain hidden during visual review because the text itself looks correct. Inspect after the content change and again after loading the translated URL directly. A passing check requires a programmatically determinable language that reflects the actual content; a language dropdown or a flag is not a substitute. Language support varies across synthesizers, so document both the markup result and the voice used rather than treating an absent voice as proof that the attribute is wrong.
Review a second case

Review case: A university publishes an English application form and a separate Japanese translation. Both are generated from the same template, which hard-codes lang="en". A screenshot of the Japanese version looks correct, yet the inherited language metadata remains English. Change the template to receive the page language from the translation data, and verify that it sets the root attribute on a direct load as well as when navigating from English. Inspect any application shell that stays in English separately: the language of a part may need different markup. Do not derive the document language only from the user’s browser preferences, since those preferences can differ from the content actually displayed. Compare the accessible language exposed for the root with the visible page content and record the route used to reach the page. This evidence distinguishes an incorrectly configured translation from a missing speech voice.
Implementation and verification

A multilingual application may replace its main content without loading a new document. When the predominant language changes, update the root language as part of the transition; when only a widget changes, mark that widget instead. Inspect the rendered document after navigation, not just the server template. A visitor's preferred language may differ from the article's actual language. Store the editorial language with each translation so a new locale does not require a developer to guess. Distinguish incorrect metadata from an unavailable speech voice: both affect the experience, but fixing one does not establish the other is available.

Review the published page and the learner's real task rather than an isolated sample. Record the relevant passage, its context, and how someone finds the explanation or language information. Inspect information exposed to software as well as the visible text. Test a representative route with keyboard and assistive technology where relevant. A successful test establishes what happened on that route; it does not prove every translation, speech voice, or later content update is correct. Recheck when editors change a passage, glossary entry, or translation, and record the result for the specific page and version reviewed.
Knowledge check
Which markup identifies the default language of an English page? Consider the consequences of each approach before continuing.
Required practical activity

Inspect two pages with different main languages. Record the root lang value, compare it with the predominant text, and correct any mismatch. Record the barrier, the change you made, and the evidence from your test.
Key takeaway
A language tag on the root identifies the human language of the page. Consult the complete WCAG 2.2 criterion for its scope and exceptions.
Reference: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/

lessons.title: 3.1.2 Language of Parts
lessons.objective: Mark passages whose human language differs from the page

content.text: Learning objectives
Mark passages whose human language differs from the page. This lesson addresses WCAG 2.2 3.1.2 Language of Parts (Level AA).
Why this matters

When a sentence switches from English to French, a synthesizer may continue applying English pronunciation unless the passage identifies its language. Language information is programmatic, so it can help speech and other tools without relying on a visual flag.
How to apply the criterion

Mark a meaningful foreign-language passage with a language tag, such as Bonjour inside an English page. Apply it to the appropriate phrase, not an unrelated container. The criterion has exceptions for proper names, technical terms, indeterminate language, and words or phrases that have become part of the surrounding language.
Real-world example

A recipe written in English quotes a full French sentence. Without a language change, a speech synthesizer may apply English pronunciation to the quotation. Put lang="fr" on the quotation while leaving the surrounding English under the document language.
The chef says: Bon appétit !

The language attribute inherits through nested elements. Place it on the smallest meaningful passage, and avoid wrapping later English text. Proper names, technical terms, indeterminate language, and words that have become part of the surrounding language are exceptions in the criterion. Whether a term qualifies depends on context; do not mark every borrowed word automatically.
Review and testing

Do not assume every borrowed word needs a language change. Review the context and applicable exceptions. Test the page with language switching enabled and check that the surrounding English resumes afterward. A visual label alone does not expose the language of the passage programmatically.
Language changes within components

A language switch can occur inside a button name, a heading, or a quotation. Place the language attribute on the element containing the translated passage, and verify the attribute remains present after the framework renders or updates the page. Nested attributes can switch back to the surrounding language if a passage contains another embedded language.

A product name in a different language is not automatically a failure: proper names and technical terms are among the stated exceptions. Consider a name that is also an ordinary foreign-language sentence separately rather than applying a blanket rule. Inspect the accessibility tree and listen to a representative passage; pronunciation depends on available speech voices and language-switching settings.
Scope and inheritance

Language attributes are inherited, so place a change on the smallest element that contains the passage in the other language. If a whole quotation is French, mark the quotation rather than every word. If the quotation contains a nested English phrase, that phrase may need its own language declaration so that the inherited French does not continue through it.

An interface that uses a flag icon to indicate language can help sighted readers, but an icon does not set pronunciation rules for text. Inspect the actual element containing the words. When testing with speech, verify both the foreign passage and the return to the surrounding language; an available voice and language-switching settings can affect the result.
Walkthrough: a quotation in a multilingual lesson

Start with an English document whose root declares English. Insert a complete French quotation within an English paragraph, then put the French language tag on the element enclosing the quotation. The surrounding words inherit English from the document; the quotation inherits French from its enclosing element. Keep punctuation associated with the quoted passage within the same logical boundary so the markup describes the text rather than an arbitrary visual span.

Use browser inspection to verify the attribute is attached to the text that actually appears. With language switching enabled in a screen reader, listen before, during, and after the quotation. If the speech voice does not change, verify whether a suitable voice is installed before assuming that the markup failed. If French pronunciation continues into the next English sentence, inspect whether the French element accidentally wraps too much content.

Review common exceptions in context. Proper names, technical terms, words of indeterminate language, and words that have become part of the immediately surrounding language are treated differently by the criterion. Do not mark an entire English paragraph as French just because it contains one phrase, and do not assume a colored flag supplies a programmatic language. Record the boundaries and the speech configuration used for testing.
Apply the distinction

Consider a travel article with a French greeting, a personal name, and a technical product name in the same paragraph. The French greeting may require a language change; the name and technical term need contextual review because the criterion contains exceptions. Do not make the entire paragraph French merely to accommodate the greeting. Conversely, marking only the first word of a complete French quotation can cause the remaining words to inherit the English page language. Inspect the final rendered markup after any translation or content-management updates, then read across the boundary. The observation to record is which passage has which inherited language, including whether the surrounding language resumes.
Review a second case

Review case: A course in English contains a German quotation followed by an English explanation. The author puts lang="de" on a container that wraps both paragraphs. A screen reader that uses language changes can apply German pronunciation to the English explanation as well. Move the language attribute onto the quotation itself, inspect the resulting nesting, and verify that the English explanation again inherits the page default. A visual heading such as “German quotation” does not itself expose the language of the quoted words. If the quotation contains a proper name, assess the criterion’s exception in context rather than indiscriminately marking individual words. Test the boundary after content has been saved through the editor: exported markup can differ from the initial source. The goal is that software can determine the language of the relevant passage, not that every reader must use a particular voice.
Implementation and verification

Consider a French quotation with an English passage nested inside it. Mark the quotation and the nested passage at their actual boundaries so inherited language follows the content. Avoid applying French to an enclosing section that also contains English instructions. Check the rendered output after an editor saves and publishes it: markup can be lost during conversion. Review the criterion's exceptions for proper names, technical terms, indeterminate language, and words incorporated into the surrounding language before treating them as failures. A speech test helps find errors, but the requirement concerns programmatic identification rather than guaranteeing a particular voice.

Review the published page and the learner's real task rather than an isolated sample. Record the relevant passage, its context, and how someone finds the explanation or language information. Inspect information exposed to software as well as the visible text. Test a representative route with keyboard and assistive technology where relevant. A successful test establishes what happened on that route; it does not prove every translation, speech voice, or later content update is correct. Recheck when editors change a passage, glossary entry, or translation, and record the result for the specific page and version reviewed.
Knowledge check
How can a French quotation in an English page identify its language? Consider the consequences of each approach before continuing.
Required practical activity

Create a paragraph with an English sentence and a French quotation. Mark the quotation, inspect the resulting DOM, and listen with a screen reader. Record the barrier, the change you made, and the evidence from your test.
Key takeaway
The lang attribute supplies a machine-readable language tag. Consult the complete WCAG 2.2 criterion for its scope and exceptions.
Reference: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/

lessons.title: 3.1.3 Unusual Words
lessons.objective: Provide a way to identify meanings of unusual words

content.text: Learning objectives
Provide a way to identify meanings of unusual words. This lesson addresses WCAG 2.2 3.1.3 Unusual Words (Level AAA).
Why this matters

Specialist terms, idioms, and words used in a restricted sense can prevent readers from understanding content even when each word is pronounced correctly. A technical student may understand a word differently from a specialist audience. This AAA criterion asks for a mechanism to identify intended definitions in the relevant cases.
How to apply the criterion

Provide a contextual definition, a glossary, or a linked explanation. For example, after first using “token” in an authentication lesson, explain whether it means a temporary credential or a physical object. Place help where readers can find it without losing their place.
Real-world example

In a course on security, the word “salt” has a technical meaning distinct from a kitchen ingredient. A link to a general dictionary may lead to the wrong definition. Introduce the precise meaning in the lesson or link directly to a glossary entry.
A salt is a unique value added before hashing a password. See the glossary entry for salt.

An explanation must be discoverable without a pointing device and must reflect the sense used in this passage. Link the term to an actual definition on the same page or a maintained glossary. A definition that only repeats the term does not clarify its meaning. Avoid unexplained jargon in the definition itself.
Review and testing

A dictionary link is not always enough when the intended meaning is a domain-specific sense. Check that the definition matches the way the word is used, and keep glossary links accessible from keyboard and assistive technology. Common terms do not automatically become unusual words merely because they appear in a technical article.
Choosing an explanation

A security lesson might use “salt” both as a general word and as a technical term. Define the technical sense where that meaning first matters; use an anchor that points to a real glossary entry when the explanation is longer. An in-page definition saves navigation, while a glossary can consolidate longer definitions shared across lessons. Both need clear, accessible links and accurate content.

Review expressions whose meaning cannot be inferred from ordinary usage, including idioms used metaphorically. An explanation must clarify the intended sense in that passage, not simply repeat the expression. Ask a learner to describe the term in their own words and trace the glossary link with keyboard and screen reader. This is a content review as well as a link test.
Choosing a useful definition

A definition is most useful when it explains a word in the same sense as the current task. For example, in a course about accounts, a session is the period during which an authenticated interaction is maintained, not a meeting in a classroom. Introduce that meaning where the term first becomes relevant and link it to a glossary if readers may encounter it later without the introduction.

Check the definition in the context of a real instruction. Ask a learner to describe what expires when the page says a session has expired. If the learner can read the definition but still cannot understand the action, revise the surrounding explanation as well. Do not hide essential meaning exclusively behind a tooltip that requires a mouse.
Walkthrough: defining a term in a security course

A lesson might say “The token expires after ten minutes.” A newcomer may know token as a physical object and not understand that this lesson uses it for a temporary credential. Introduce the intended meaning in the surrounding text: a token is a value that a service uses to recognize or authorize a request. Explain expiration in the next sentence, including what the learner should do when it occurs.

If the term appears across many lessons, add a glossary entry and a descriptive link. Test the link from the keyboard and make sure the learner can return to the sentence without losing context. A glossary that lists several unrelated meanings but does not identify the sense used in the lesson leaves the original ambiguity unresolved. An icon with an unexplained tooltip also fails to provide a dependable route for every user.

Now review idioms and phrases used in a restricted meaning, not just technical nouns. Ask a reader unfamiliar with the domain to explain a representative instruction in their own words. Revise the definition if it requires further unexplained jargon. Confirm that the definition is accurate for this course rather than promising a universal meaning that the term does not have.
Apply the distinction

Imagine documentation says that a user must “revoke a token” without explaining either term. A useful explanation identifies the token as a credential and explains that revocation makes it unusable; it also tells the user the practical consequence for an existing integration. Simply replacing “revoke” with “invalidate” may exchange one unfamiliar term for another. Present the explanation close to the instruction or supply a reliable glossary mechanism, and make sure the link text identifies the term. Ask a novice what will happen to requests using the token after revocation. Their answer can reveal whether the definition communicates the intended restricted meaning rather than merely repeating the same unfamiliar word.
Review a second case

Review case: A tutorial tells a student to “roll back the migration” but offers only a dictionary definition of roll as movement. In this context, a rollback means reversing a database change, and the exact effect depends on the migration. Explain the intended technical sense, then state which operation the student should perform and what result to expect. If a glossary provides the definition, make the link meaningful and reachable without hover; place enough context in the surrounding instructions that a learner can decide when to consult it. Test the wording with someone who has not previously worked with migrations. Ask them to distinguish rolling back a change from deleting the entire database. Revise the entry if it is technically misleading or only substitutes more specialized vocabulary. A definition mechanism must supply the intended meaning, not simply a list of possible unrelated senses.
Implementation and verification

A glossary must define the sense used in the lesson, not merely list unrelated dictionary meanings. For example, clarify that a security challenge is a prompt used to verify identity when that is the intended sense. Place a short explanation where the word matters or link directly to an appropriate glossary entry. Verify the link target, keyboard access, and a clear way back to the passage. Ask a learner unfamiliar with the topic to explain the word in context. That exercise can reveal circular definitions which repeat the unfamiliar term without explaining it.

Review the published page and the learner's real task rather than an isolated sample. Record the relevant passage, its context, and how someone finds the explanation or language information. Inspect information exposed to software as well as the visible text. Test a representative route with keyboard and assistive technology where relevant. A successful test establishes what happened on that route; it does not prove every translation, speech voice, or later content update is correct. Recheck when editors change a passage, glossary entry, or translation, and record the result for the specific page and version reviewed.
Knowledge check
What makes a glossary useful for a specialized term? Consider the consequences of each approach before continuing.
Required practical activity

Choose three technical or idiomatic terms in a page. Write context-specific definitions and link each to an accessible glossary or explanation. Record the barrier, the change you made, and the evidence from your test.
Key takeaway
The reader needs the meaning used by the content. Consult the complete WCAG 2.2 criterion for its scope and exceptions.
Reference: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/

lessons.title: 3.1.4 Abbreviations
lessons.objective: Provide a mechanism for identifying expansions of abbreviations

content.text: Learning objectives
Provide a mechanism for identifying expansions of abbreviations. This lesson addresses WCAG 2.2 3.1.4 Abbreviations (Level AAA).
Why this matters

Abbreviations save space but may hide meaning from a reader encountering a subject for the first time. An abbreviation may have several expansions; for example, “API” is recognizable to some developers but unfamiliar to new students.
How to apply the criterion

Give the expansion at first use or provide an accessible glossary. “Application programming interface (API)” makes the relationship explicit. An abbr element with an appropriate title may help some users, but title display and assistive technology support vary, so visible expansion is a reliable approach.
Real-world example

A student sees “DOM” in an introductory lesson for the first time. Using the abbreviation repeatedly without expansion forces them to search elsewhere and choose between different possible meanings. The expansion near the first use makes the lesson self-contained.
The Document Object Model (DOM) represents the page as a tree of nodes.

If the expansion appears in a glossary instead, make the glossary available using an accessible link. An abbreviation that is part of the language may fall under the criterion’s exception. An abbr title alone can be difficult to discover with touch or keyboard, so visible expansion can be more useful even where other techniques are supported.
Review and testing

Do not rely only on a mouse hover tooltip. Readers using touch, keyboard, or speech may not discover it. This AAA criterion includes exceptions for abbreviations that are part of the language; check the complete requirement and context before concluding that an expansion is necessary.
Repeated abbreviations and navigation

A long course may introduce an abbreviation on one page and use it again on another. Readers can enter on the second page from a search result, so a page-level expansion or glossary link can be more useful than relying on an explanation in an earlier lesson. If the same letters have different meanings in different fields, provide the expansion that matches the current usage.

Acronyms can be understandable to experienced developers while confusing new students. Expand them without making the sentence unnecessarily difficult: write the full phrase first, then the abbreviation in parentheses. Check touch and keyboard access if a tooltip supplements that explanation. The requirement allows specified exceptions, so assess the actual abbreviation rather than assuming every shortened form needs identical treatment.
First use and repeated entry points

A learner may enter documentation through a search result and never see the first occurrence on the home page. Consider how each page can provide an expansion or a reachable glossary, particularly when a shortened term is central to an instruction. The same abbreviation can mean different things in different fields, so choose the expansion that fits the current subject.

A visible expansion supports readers even when browser or assistive-technology support for title tooltips varies. If a glossary link is used, give it a meaningful name and make sure it can be followed and returned from with the keyboard. Review labels and compact navigation too: shortening a control name without explaining it can make the action hard to identify.
Walkthrough: introducing abbreviations in documentation

A page instructs learners to call an API, but a reader arriving from search may never have seen the expansion. On the first relevant occurrence in that page, write “application programming interface (API)” and explain its role in the task. If multiple abbreviations share the same letters, make the intended expansion explicit rather than linking to a list of unrelated possibilities.

For a long manual, a searchable glossary can supplement first-use explanations. Each entry should identify the abbreviation and its meaning in context. A table of expansions must have understandable headings and be reachable through a descriptive link. Check repeated interface labels too: a compact menu item may be the reader’s first encounter even when the document text explains the term later.

Try the page with a mouse, keyboard, and touch input. A browser tooltip shown only on hover is easy to miss and may not be consistently exposed by assistive technologies; do not rely on it as the only mechanism. Check the criterion’s exceptions for abbreviations that have become part of the language instead of mechanically expanding every shortened word.
Apply the distinction

Suppose an application uses “SSO” in a navigation label and defines single sign-on only in an introductory article. A learner landing directly on a settings page may never encounter that introduction. An accessible glossary, nearby expansion, or equivalent mechanism provides another way to identify the expansion in the relevant context. Check a narrow screen and a touch device, where hover-based hints may be unavailable. If a visible label is abbreviated for space, verify that a reader can still locate the expansion without guessing which icon to activate. Distinguish this requirement from defining a specialist concept: spelling out the words may still leave the concept itself in need of explanation.
Review a second case

Review case: An accessibility report uses “AT” to mean assistive technology, but a separate networking page uses the same letters for a different term. A site-wide expansion chosen without context may mislead readers. Expand the term where it is introduced in each relevant document, or provide a glossary that clearly distinguishes the meanings. Verify that a learner entering through a search result can identify the expansion without first finding the home page. If an abbr element has a title attribute, test how the expansion is encountered with keyboard, touch, and a screen reader; visible text or a reachable explanation avoids depending entirely on a hover tooltip. Expansion and comprehension are related but distinct: spelling out “assistive technology” may still require a short explanation that it refers to tools used to interact with content.
Implementation and verification

An abbreviation can have different expansions in different fields. Choose the expansion appropriate to the sentence and make it available to readers who enter directly at that page. An accessible glossary can support recurring terms, but its links should identify their targets and work without a mouse. If a supplementary definition appears in a popover, check that keyboard and touch users can open and dismiss it. Do not assume the title attribute on an abbreviation is reliably discoverable on every device. Check the stated exceptions before requiring expansions of familiar language forms.

Review the published page and the learner's real task rather than an isolated sample. Record the relevant passage, its context, and how someone finds the explanation or language information. Inspect information exposed to software as well as the visible text. Test a representative route with keyboard and assistive technology where relevant. A successful test establishes what happened on that route; it does not prove every translation, speech voice, or later content update is correct. Recheck when editors change a passage, glossary entry, or translation, and record the result for the specific page and version reviewed.
Knowledge check
What is a useful first occurrence of an unfamiliar abbreviation? Consider the consequences of each approach before continuing.
Required practical activity

Review a documentation page for abbreviations. Expand each applicable abbreviation in context and verify that the meaning can be reached without a mouse. Record the barrier, the change you made, and the evidence from your test.
Key takeaway
The expansion is directly available in the surrounding text. Consult the complete WCAG 2.2 criterion for its scope and exceptions.
Reference: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/

lessons.title: 3.1.5 Reading Level
lessons.objective: Recognize when a reading-level alternative is needed

content.text: Learning objectives
Recognize when a reading-level alternative is needed. This lesson addresses WCAG 2.2 3.1.5 Reading Level (Level AAA).
Why this matters

Dense sentences and specialized vocabulary can exclude readers with cognitive or language disabilities and people new to a topic. A technically accurate page can still be hard to understand. The AAA criterion concerns text requiring reading ability more advanced than the lower secondary education level, after removing proper names and titles.
How to apply the criterion

Provide supplemental content or a version that does not require reading ability above that level when the criterion applies. A plain-language summary, a diagram with accessible explanation, or an alternative version can help, provided it preserves the information needed for the task. Do not assume that shortening a page automatically makes it understandable.
Real-world example

A benefits application explains an appeal using several long sentences and unfamiliar legal expressions. A plain-language version can explain the deadline and next step, while retaining the original details. Compare both versions so the shorter version does not accidentally omit the right to appeal.

Plain-language summary

If you disagree, send an appeal by the date on your notice.

The criterion applies where text requires reading ability more advanced than lower secondary education after proper names and titles are removed. Supplemental content or a version below that threshold is required in the applicable case. A readability score may guide editing but cannot reliably establish whether a person understands the task; test comprehension with readers.
Review and testing

Compare the original and alternative for omissions, undefined terms, and actionable details. Ask representative readers to explain the instructions or complete a task. Automated readability formulas can flag difficult passages but do not establish understanding or replace assessment of the criterion and its exceptions.
Evaluating a simpler version

Reading difficulty is not a measure of intelligence or a reason to remove important details. Break a complex requirement into steps, define essential vocabulary, and retain conditions and deadlines. A visual explanation can help some readers, but it needs a text alternative that conveys its information. If a simplified version is provided, keep it current whenever the authoritative original changes.

Ask a reader to perform a real task with the explanation, such as identifying what document to submit and when. Note hesitations and incorrect assumptions, then revise. Readability formulas can suggest passages to inspect, but a numerical score alone is not a reliable accessibility verdict. The criterion uses lower secondary education as the threshold after removing proper names and titles.
Designing an alternative

Begin by identifying what the reader needs to decide or do. Separate conditions, actions, and consequences into a sequence, then define unavoidable specialized words. For example, explain which document a student must upload, when it is due, and what happens if it is missing. A short summary that omits one of these requirements is not an effective substitute for the complete instruction.

Supplemental material may include an accessible illustration or a worked example, but it should correspond to the original information. Invite a reader unfamiliar with the process to perform a representative task and explain the result. A readability score may reveal long sentences; it cannot determine whether a particular instruction is accurate, complete, or understandable.
Walkthrough: rewriting an enrollment instruction

Consider a paragraph that combines eligibility, a deadline, a document requirement, and a consequence for late submission in one long sentence. Identify each obligation before simplifying. A plain-language alternative might explain who can apply, list the required document, give the deadline with its time zone, and describe what happens after submission. A shorter paragraph that omits the deadline is easier to read but not a faithful explanation.

Use concrete verbs and define specialized terms at the point they are needed. Break a sequence into logical steps and show a worked example if that helps the learner understand how a rule applies. Preserve important exceptions and distinguish a requirement from a recommendation. If a diagram communicates the process, provide its information in accessible text as well so that the supplemental material is not limited to vision.

Ask a learner unfamiliar with the process to locate the deadline and explain the next action using the alternative. Compare their answers with the original and revise unclear wording. A readability calculator can flag difficult passages, but it cannot establish that the required details are present or that readers can complete the task. The WCAG criterion is conditional and includes treatment of proper names and titles; evaluate the actual text.
Apply the distinction

A useful comparison exercise is to give two readers the original policy and the supplemental version separately, then ask each to identify eligibility, required documents, and the deadline. Record differences in their answers, and check omissions against the source policy. A diagram can show the sequence of steps, but its labels, relationships, and meaningful content need an accessible text equivalent. Maintain both versions when the policy changes; a stale plain-language explanation can cause harm even if it is easy to read. Remember that the criterion specifies a reading-ability threshold and permits supplemental content or a qualifying version: shorter text alone does not establish that the condition has been met.
Review a second case

Review case: A policy states that applications received after a certain date may be considered only if the department approves an exception. A simplified version that says “Late applications are accepted” changes the policy. Preserve the condition and explain who makes the decision, what the applicant should submit, and how the decision will be communicated when those details are available. If the original is uncertain or incomplete, do not invent a promise in the alternative. Ask a new learner to identify the standard deadline and describe the exception using both versions. Check whether a diagram or example includes the same condition, and provide its essential information in text. A readability formula can highlight complexity but cannot verify that the policy’s conditions and consequences remain accurate. Maintain the supplemental version when the original changes.
Implementation and verification

A plain-language version must retain the conditions needed to complete the task. If an enrollment policy gives new and returning students different deadlines, name both groups and dates; saying only “apply early” loses the distinction. Break instructions into steps and explain unavoidable technical terms. Keep the alternative current when policy changes. Ask a representative reader to identify the correct deadline and documents rather than asking only whether the page looks simple. The lower-secondary threshold is a criterion for text, not a measure of a person's intelligence. A readability score alone does not establish understanding.

Review the published page and the learner's real task rather than an isolated sample. Record the relevant passage, its context, and how someone finds the explanation or language information. Inspect information exposed to software as well as the visible text. Test a representative route with keyboard and assistive technology where relevant. A successful test establishes what happened on that route; it does not prove every translation, speech voice, or later content update is correct. Recheck when editors change a passage, glossary entry, or translation, and record the result for the specific page and version reviewed.
Knowledge check
What can help when text requires a reading ability above the specified level? Consider the consequences of each approach before continuing.
Required practical activity

Rewrite a complex enrollment instruction in plain language. Ask a reader to locate the deadline and required documents in both versions, and revise any ambiguity. Record the barrier, the change you made, and the evidence from your test.
Key takeaway
The alternative needs to make the original content understandable without losing task information. Consult the complete WCAG 2.2 criterion for its scope and exceptions.
Reference: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/

lessons.title: 3.1.6 Pronunciation
lessons.objective: Provide pronunciation where meaning depends on it

content.text: Learning objectives
Provide pronunciation where meaning depends on it. This lesson addresses WCAG 2.2 3.1.6 Pronunciation (Level AAA).
Why this matters

Some words are spelled the same but pronounced differently depending on meaning. A synthesizer or reader may choose the wrong pronunciation when context alone is insufficient. This can alter meaning even when the spelling is correct.
How to apply the criterion

Provide a way to determine the intended pronunciation for words whose meaning is ambiguous without it. Depending on the content, a pronunciation guide, phonetic text, or accessible audio can supply the information. Make the guide available alongside the relevant word or through a clear link.
Real-world example

An instructional sentence contains a word whose spelling permits two pronunciations with different meanings. If context does not resolve the ambiguity, readers need a way to determine the intended pronunciation. A short textual pronunciation guide adjacent to that occurrence can clarify the intended sense.
Please record (ri-KORD) the result in your notebook.

A guide should be accurate for the intended language and dialect and understandable to its audience. Where phonetic notation is used, explain the notation or provide another accessible form. The criterion is not a requirement to annotate every word; it targets words whose meaning is ambiguous without pronunciation.
Review and testing

Do not provide only audio without considering people who cannot hear it; a written pronunciation guide may also be useful. A recording should itself be accessible through appropriate alternatives. Check with language specialists where a pronunciation or notation is uncertain.
Clarifying meaning without relying on sound

An audio recording can demonstrate pronunciation, but it is not sufficient help for someone who cannot hear it. A readable pronunciation guide can accompany audio. Different dialects may pronounce the same word differently, so state the intended meaning and use a notation familiar to the audience; ask a language specialist to check difficult examples.

Do not assume that a speech synthesizer will infer the intended pronunciation correctly from surrounding words. Test the specific occurrence and verify that the learner can locate its guide. The criterion concerns words whose meaning is ambiguous without knowing their pronunciation, not every uncommon spelling. A definition and a pronunciation guide solve related but distinct problems.
Meaning, context and pronunciation

A pronunciation guide needs to identify the word in its actual sentence. For example, “record” can refer to a stored item or the action of recording, with different stress patterns in English. If the sentence already makes the intended meaning clear, the specific ambiguity addressed by this criterion may not arise; evaluate the passage instead of adding phonetic text to every occurrence.

If audio is offered, check that a learner can find and operate it without a mouse. Written phonetic guidance or a clear explanation can help someone who cannot hear the recording. Verify pronunciation with a reliable language specialist and test whether the explanation communicates the intended sense to the intended audience.
Walkthrough: identifying an ambiguous pronunciation

Write two sentences using “record”: one asks a learner to record a video, while the other refers to a record of the result. The word has different pronunciation patterns in those uses. Ask whether the surrounding sentence already makes the intended meaning clear. The criterion is concerned with cases where meaning is ambiguous unless the pronunciation is known, not with adding guides to every word with several pronunciations.

Where a guide is needed, connect it to the exact occurrence. A written guide can describe the stressed syllable or use a notation appropriate for the intended audience; an audio example can supplement that explanation. Make a linked guide discoverable and operable with keyboard and touch, and avoid requiring a reader to interpret a notation they have not been taught.

Test the explanation with someone who has not seen the example before. Can they distinguish the intended action from the noun? If audio is present, verify the recording is clear and the control is labeled; ensure a usable text-based explanation is available for a learner who cannot hear it. Consult language expertise where the pronunciation or meaning is uncertain.
Apply the distinction

Suppose an audio pronunciation button sits beside an ambiguous word. Its accessible name should identify what will play, such as “Hear pronunciation of record,” rather than only “Play.” A keyboard user must be able to operate it and a listener must be able to distinguish the relevant pronunciation. Provide a readable guide or explanation where sound is not available to the learner. Evaluate whether the spelling is genuinely ambiguous in that particular sentence: a guide may not be necessary where the context already communicates meaning, while an isolated vocabulary list can require more explanation. Review the accuracy of any phonetic notation and explain the notation if the intended audience may not recognize it.
Review a second case

Review case: A vocabulary exercise presents the isolated word “lead” and asks which meaning it has. Without more context, a reader may need to know whether the intended pronunciation denotes a metal or the action of guiding. Supply a context-specific pronunciation or meaning mechanism beside that occurrence. A written stress or sound guide may be easier for some readers to use than a recording, while a recording may help others; choose an explanation suited to the audience and make any control clearly labeled. Test the guidance with a learner who has not heard the instructor’s spoken explanation. If the sentence already unambiguously establishes the intended sense, assess whether this criterion’s condition is met rather than mechanically adding the same pronunciation widget everywhere. Confirm the guide remains accurate when the example is translated.
Implementation and verification

Attach pronunciation guidance to the occurrence where meaning would otherwise be ambiguous. If the same spelling has different meanings elsewhere, a generic link may leave the reader unsure which pronunciation applies. A written guide can complement audio for someone who cannot hear the recording. A notation familiar to specialists may be opaque to beginners, so explain it or offer a familiar equivalent. Check difficult examples with someone knowledgeable about the language and audience, particularly where pronunciation varies by region. The criterion addresses meaning dependent on pronunciation, not every unfamiliar word.

Review the published page and the learner's real task rather than an isolated sample. Record the relevant passage, its context, and how someone finds the explanation or language information. Inspect information exposed to software as well as the visible text. Test a representative route with keyboard and assistive technology where relevant. A successful test establishes what happened on that route; it does not prove every translation, speech voice, or later content update is correct. Recheck when editors change a passage, glossary entry, or translation, and record the result for the specific page and version reviewed.
Knowledge check
When is a pronunciation mechanism particularly relevant? Consider the consequences of each approach before continuing.
Required practical activity

Find a word whose intended meaning changes with pronunciation in a sample sentence. Add a pronunciation guide and test whether a reader can identify the intended meaning. Record the barrier, the change you made, and the evidence from your test.
Key takeaway
The criterion addresses ambiguity that depends on pronunciation. Consult the complete WCAG 2.2 criterion for its scope and exceptions.
Reference: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/

lessons.title: 3.2.1 On Focus
lessons.objective: Avoid unexpected context changes on focus

content.text: Learning objectives
Avoid unexpected context changes on focus. This lesson addresses WCAG 2.2 3.2.1 On Focus (Level A).
Why this matters

Focus identifies the interface element currently ready for keyboard interaction. Merely moving focus to a control should not unexpectedly take a person to another page, submit a form, or open a new window. Such changes can disorient keyboard and screen-reader users who are exploring rather than choosing.
How to apply the criterion

Separate focus from activation. A menu item can receive focus without navigating; navigation occurs after an intentional action such as pressing Enter or clicking. Showing a non-disruptive focus indicator or updating a small description is not necessarily a change of context.
Real-world example

A menu item triggers location.assign when it receives focus. A keyboard user presses Tab to find the next control, but the browser immediately navigates away. Replace the focus handler with an ordinary link so focus and activation remain separate.
Courses

A native link is activated intentionally; reaching it with Tab should not navigate. Check both keyboard and script-driven focus. Showing a focus ring is expected and helpful, while a substantial context change such as navigating to another page on focus is the issue. An example alone cannot establish whether the surrounding page conforms.
Review and testing

A focus event can be caused by keyboard navigation, script, or assistive technology. Do not attach a redirect to onfocus. Test with Tab and Shift+Tab from the start of the page and observe whether the location, focus, or whole view changes unexpectedly.
Focus, activation and state updates

Focus may arrive through Tab, a screen reader command, or a script that returns the user to a validation error. A redirect attached to the focus event can therefore interrupt navigation in several ways. Remove the redirect and trigger the consequential action from an explicit link or button instead. Retaining visible focus helps users understand where they are before deciding to activate anything.

A tooltip or focus styling is not automatically a change of context. Evaluate the actual result: did the page navigate, open a new window, move focus elsewhere, or otherwise substantially change the user’s interaction? Test both forward and backward keyboard navigation, and verify the browser location and active element before and after focus arrives.
Focus is not activation

Keyboard focus is a position in the interface, not a decision. Pressing Tab may move through several links before the learner chooses one. If focus itself opens a new page or submits a form, a person cannot inspect the options safely. Use the focus event for feedback such as a visible indicator, and use an explicit activation event for navigation or submission.

Test forward and backward keyboard movement through every interactive item. Also check script-driven focus after an error or dialog closes: moving focus to explain an error is different from using focus to trigger a new context. Record the starting control, action, destination, and whether navigation was intentional so the result is reproducible.
Walkthrough: repairing a focus-triggered redirect

A menu developer attaches navigation to a link’s focus event so that a destination opens as soon as the link receives keyboard focus. Starting at the top of the page, press Tab until that link is reached. The page changes before Enter is pressed, preventing the learner from examining the remaining options. This is a different action from a visible focus outline or a brief description appearing near the control.

Remove the redirect from the focus handler. Keep a semantic link with a real destination, and allow the browser’s normal activation behavior to follow it when the user chooses the link. If JavaScript is needed, attach the consequential operation to activation rather than focus. Check that clicking still works and that keyboard focus remains visible while moving through the menu.

Test Tab and Shift+Tab across the whole menu and verify that the address, open window, and focused element do not change context merely because focus moved. Then activate the intended link and confirm the destination. Repeat after a dialog closes or validation returns focus to a field, because programmatically moved focus can also trigger a problematic handler.
Apply the distinction

A second failure pattern occurs in a form that opens a new window whenever a field receives focus. A learner tabbing through the form may be repeatedly interrupted even though they have made no choice. Replace that behavior with a labeled Help button, and make the new window or dialog behavior clear as appropriate. Test with a pointer too, because clicking a field can also place focus there. Note that focus can intentionally be moved by a script, such as focusing an error summary after submission; assess whether receiving focus itself initiates a further context change. A focus indicator is feedback about location and is not, by itself, the disruptive transition addressed here.
Review a second case

Review case: A search result opens its detail page as soon as the result receives focus. This may appear convenient when using a mouse, but a keyboard user cannot pass through the result list to explore other choices. Replace the focus-triggered navigation with a standard link whose destination opens on activation. Starting before the list, tab through all results and back with Shift+Tab. Record whether the URL, active window, or focus location changes before an explicit activation. Then activate one link and verify that it reaches the correct page. Also inspect event handlers added by third-party components; disabling a handler in the visible template will not fix the interaction if another listener still redirects. Showing a focus outline or a small explanatory hint is different from moving the learner to a new context.
Implementation and verification

Test the actual workflow rather than searching for one event handler. Move to the control using Tab, move away with Shift+Tab, and repeat when a validation script returns focus to it. Record whether the URL, window, or focus position changes before activation. A focus ring or tooltip does not automatically constitute a context change. Replace a focus-triggered redirect with an explicit link or button, then test its keyboard activation. Confirm the accessible name describes the action or destination, so the user can decide whether to activate it.

Start at a realistic entry point and record the user's actions and resulting changes. Compare visible presentation with DOM order, keyboard route, accessible names, and any user preference relevant to the case. Test the default view and a narrow viewport when the same mechanism appears in both. Note whether the user initiated a change: an intentional selection and an unexpected transition create different experiences. Retest after modifying a shared component, since an older template may still exhibit the original problem. Record the specific pages, interaction steps, expected behavior, and actual behavior so another reviewer can reproduce the finding.
Knowledge check
What should happen when a navigation link receives focus? Consider the consequences of each approach before continuing.
Required practical activity

Tab through a navigation menu and form. Record any focus-triggered context change, then revise the control so the user explicitly activates the action. Record the barrier, the change you made, and the evidence from your test.
Key takeaway
Moving focus is not the same as choosing a destination. Consult the complete WCAG 2.2 criterion for its scope and exceptions.
Reference: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/

lessons.title: 3.2.2 On Input
lessons.objective: Make the effect of changing a control predictable

content.text: Learning objectives
Make the effect of changing a control predictable. This lesson addresses WCAG 2.2 3.2.2 On Input (Level A).
Why this matters

A user may change a value while reviewing options, using a keyboard, or entering data. If the change immediately submits a form or moves to another page without advance warning, the result can interrupt that work. A change of context is more significant than an ordinary update within the current view.
How to apply the criterion

Use an explicit Apply, Search, or Continue button for consequential changes, or clearly inform the user of the behavior before they interact. For example, a language selector that changes pages immediately needs advance notice when that behavior causes a context change.
Real-world example

A course filter redirects on every select change. Arrow-key users may trigger navigation while moving through options. An explicit submit action lets them inspect and revise their choice before the application changes context.

<form action="/courses">
  <label for="level">Level</label>
  <select id="level" name="level"><option>Beginner</option><option>Advanced</option></select>
  <button type="submit">Apply filter</button>
</form>

If a change of setting will cause a change of context, an alternative is to inform users before the control is used. Keep the notice near the control and available programmatically. Updating results in place does not necessarily change context, but unexpected focus moves, navigation, or submission need careful evaluation.
Review and testing

A select element with an onchange redirect can make arrow-key exploration trigger navigation. Test the actual keyboard behavior and announce instructions before the control. Updating a nearby price without moving focus or navigating is not automatically the same as a context change.
Handling selectors and automatic updates

A selector may change a preview in the current page without moving focus; a selector that submits an entire form or changes location creates a different experience. Record the effect rather than assuming every input event is a context change. An explicit Apply button is often easier to understand, particularly when a user wants to compare several options before committing.

If the design intentionally changes context as soon as a setting changes, inform the user before they interact with that control. A warning shown only after selection comes too late. Test using keyboard arrows and screen reader interaction as well as pointer input. Check that a user can change their selection without accidentally losing other form entries.
Distinguishing input from commitment

A learner can change a selection as part of exploring choices. If the application immediately sends them to another page on the first arrow-key change, the learner may never reach the desired option. A separate Apply button makes the commitment explicit, while text before the control can describe an immediate context change when that behavior is intended.

Not every live update is a context change. A filter that updates a list in place without moving focus or navigating needs accessibility review, including announcement of important results, but should not automatically be treated as the same case as a redirect. Test with keyboard, pointer, and assistive technology, and observe the actual change rather than judging from the event name alone.
Walkthrough: a language selector

Suppose a selector immediately navigates to another language version whenever its value changes. A keyboard user may press an arrow key while exploring the options and unexpectedly leave the page. Replace the immediate redirect with a labeled selector and an Apply button, or provide clear advance information about an immediate context change where the intended design requires one.

Test from the keyboard without activating Apply. Move through several options, return to the original choice, and check that the current page and focus remain stable. Then choose a language and activate Apply; verify that the selected language and destination agree. Keep the label and any behavioral instructions available before the user operates the control.

A live update is not automatically a change of context. For instance, updating an estimated price in place without navigating or moving focus is a different interaction, though it still needs clear communication and accessible status handling. Review the behavior experienced by the learner, not simply whether the code uses an input or change event.
Apply the distinction

Consider a checkbox labeled “Send updates” that submits and reloads the entire form as soon as it is checked. A user exploring the option may lose their place or unsubmitted answers. Add an explicit Save button, preserve the other values, and verify the checkbox can be changed in both directions before saving. If the application instead updates an in-page preview while keeping focus and location stable, evaluate whether it actually changes context rather than assuming all automatic updates fail. Provide accurate instructions before any control whose input causes a consequential context change. Test the real interaction on keyboard and touch because browser behavior for select controls can vary.
Review a second case

Review case: A region selector updates the selected region locally and also immediately redirects to a new page when the value changes. A keyboard user may select an intermediate option accidentally while moving through the list. Provide an Apply button or give clear advance information when immediate navigation is intended. Verify the browser location does not change while a user explores values in the button-based design, and check that activating Apply opens the chosen region rather than a previously selected value. Do not classify every dynamic calculation as a context change: updating a displayed shipping estimate without redirecting or moving focus has different effects, though its important updates must still be communicated accessibly. Preserve unsaved entries when the application transitions, so the learner does not unexpectedly lose work.
Implementation and verification

A selector that reloads the page immediately can interrupt a keyboard user who is moving through choices. Put a clear warning before the control when a change of context occurs automatically, or provide an Apply button after the selection. Preserve other entered form values when appropriate. Test using the browser and assistive technologies supported by the product because selection behavior can differ. A small preview updated in place is not automatically a context change: observe whether the page, focus, or other substantial context actually changes before recording a failure.

Start at a realistic entry point and record the user's actions and resulting changes. Compare visible presentation with DOM order, keyboard route, accessible names, and any user preference relevant to the case. Test the default view and a narrow viewport when the same mechanism appears in both. Note whether the user initiated a change: an intentional selection and an unexpected transition create different experiences. Retest after modifying a shared component, since an older template may still exhibit the original problem. Record the specific pages, interaction steps, expected behavior, and actual behavior so another reviewer can reproduce the finding.
Knowledge check
How can a filter avoid an unexpected submission when its value changes? Consider the consequences of each approach before continuing.
Required practical activity

Build a filter with a select and an Apply button. Test choosing several options with the keyboard and confirm that navigation or submission occurs only when expected. Record the barrier, the change you made, and the evidence from your test.
Key takeaway
An explicit action makes the consequential change predictable. Consult the complete WCAG 2.2 criterion for its scope and exceptions.
Reference: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/

lessons.title: 3.2.3 Consistent Navigation
lessons.objective: Keep repeated navigation in a consistent relative order

content.text: Learning objectives
Keep repeated navigation in a consistent relative order. This lesson addresses WCAG 2.2 3.2.3 Consistent Navigation (Level AA).
Why this matters

People learn where common navigation appears and use that knowledge on later pages. If links move unpredictably, users must repeatedly search, which increases cognitive effort and slows keyboard navigation.
How to apply the criterion

For navigation mechanisms repeated across multiple pages, keep their relative order consistent unless the user initiates a change. A header with Home, Courses, and Help should preserve that sequence across pages where those links recur. Individual pages may contain additional links; relative order does not mean every page must have an identical menu.
Real-world example

The course site repeats Home, Courses, and Help in its header. On one page the order is Home, Help, Courses. A learner relying on a familiar sequence now has to search again. Restore the relative order of the repeated links across pages.
Home Courses Help

Relative order does not prohibit adding page-specific links or changing the menu when the user requests it. Compare the set of pages where the navigation recurs. A menu collapsed at a narrow viewport should still provide an understandable and consistent sequence when opened.
Review and testing

Compare pages in the same set rather than comparing unrelated applications. Responsive layouts can change visual presentation while preserving a meaningful relative order. User-selected customization is permitted by the criterion, but do not silently reorder links for everyone.
Order across pages and layouts

Suppose Courses appears between Home and Help on desktop, but a redesigned lesson template moves Help before Courses. Both pages contain all three links, yet their relative order differs. A consistent sequence helps users who navigate by position or by repeated keystrokes. A page-specific link can be added without changing the sequence of links that recur.

Responsive layouts may rearrange visual elements, collapse navigation, or expose a different source order. Test the repeated navigation in both its open mobile state and desktop presentation. A user may initiate a change in order, such as choosing a personalized menu; document the chosen state separately from unexpected template changes.
Comparing relative order

Relative order means that repeated links retain their sequence when they appear together. A page may add a local link without moving Home, Courses, and Help relative to one another. The criterion does not require every page to contain all the same links, nor does it prevent a learner from choosing a personalized order.

To review a site, select several pages within the same set and list their repeated navigation items in the order encountered. Compare both the visual presentation and keyboard sequence, particularly at narrow widths where a menu may collapse. A design that appears consistent but places repeated links in a different focus order can still confuse a keyboard user.
Walkthrough: reviewing a set of course pages

Record the header links on the course overview, lesson, and account pages. If Home, Courses, and Help are repeated, note their relative order on each page. A lesson page may insert a “Resources” link between Courses and Help without changing the relative sequence of the three repeated links. A page that moves Help ahead of Home changes the sequence a learner has already learned.

Check both desktop and narrow mobile layouts. Open the collapsed menu and use the keyboard to record the order in which repeated links receive focus. A visual layout and the DOM or focus order can diverge, so inspecting only a screenshot is not enough. Compare pages in the same set, and distinguish a user’s explicit customization from an unexplained site-wide change.

When fixing an inconsistency, adjust the shared navigation template if possible so the correction applies across pages. Recheck page-specific additions to make sure they do not reverse the repeated links. Keep a record of the pages and viewport sizes inspected. This criterion concerns consistent relative order; it does not require an identical set of links on every page.
Apply the distinction

Compare three pages that all contain Home, Courses, and Help. The sequences Home–Courses–Help and Home–Resources–Courses–Help preserve the repeated links’ relative order; Courses–Home–Help does not. A learner may use visual memory, screen-reader navigation, or repeated Tab presses to locate these items, so inspect the order presented through each relevant path. When a user chooses a customized order, do not mistake their choice for an unexplained inconsistency. Test any shared component change across several page types and responsive breakpoints; a fix to the desktop header can leave a separate mobile menu unchanged.
Review a second case

Review case: On one page, a repeated navigation sequence is Home, Courses, Help; on another, it becomes Home, Help, Courses because a mobile-specific component has a different link array. A learner who has memorized the sequence must relearn it on the second page. Consolidate the repeated links or otherwise synchronize their relative order, then compare the two pages at both wide and narrow widths. An additional page-specific item does not necessarily violate the requirement if the repeated items keep their relative positions. Check the order encountered with keyboard and screen reader, since CSS can visually rearrange elements independently of the source. If the learner explicitly reorders a personalized menu, document that user-initiated choice separately from an unexpected site-wide inconsistency.
Implementation and verification

Create an inventory of repeated navigation across several pages in the same set. Compare the relative sequence of common links rather than demanding identical screen coordinates or identical page-specific links. If Home, Courses, and Help appear in that order on one page but Help precedes Courses on another, the shared order differs. Open the mobile menu and examine keyboard order and visual presentation. Record a deliberately personalized order separately, since the criterion permits user-initiated changes. Comparing real page templates reveals discrepancies that a single screenshot cannot show.

Start at a realistic entry point and record the user's actions and resulting changes. Compare visible presentation with DOM order, keyboard route, accessible names, and any user preference relevant to the case. Test the default view and a narrow viewport when the same mechanism appears in both. Note whether the user initiated a change: an intentional selection and an unexpected transition create different experiences. Retest after modifying a shared component, since an older template may still exhibit the original problem. Record the specific pages, interaction steps, expected behavior, and actual behavior so another reviewer can reproduce the finding.
Knowledge check
What does consistent navigation primarily require? Consider the consequences of each approach before continuing.
Required practical activity

Compare the main navigation on three course pages, recording link order in the DOM and visually. Correct inconsistent ordering and recheck keyboard navigation. Record the barrier, the change you made, and the evidence from your test.
Key takeaway
The criterion concerns the relative order of repeated navigation mechanisms. Consult the complete WCAG 2.2 criterion for its scope and exceptions.
Reference: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/
