lessons.title: 3.2.4 Consistent Identification
lessons.objective: Identify components with the same function consistently

content.text: Learning objectives
Identify components with the same function consistently. This lesson addresses WCAG 2.2 3.2.4 Consistent Identification (Level AA).
Why this matters

A user transfers knowledge from one page to another. If identical functions have unrelated names or icons, a familiar action can appear to be a different action. Conversely, reusing one label for different actions can be misleading.
How to apply the criterion

Use consistent labels and accessible names for components that have the same functionality within a set of pages. For example, use “Search” consistently for the same search function rather than alternating between “Find”, “Go”, and an unlabeled magnifier.
Real-world example

The search function appears on two pages. One control has visible text “Search” and the other is a magnifier announced as “Submit”; both perform the same search. Align their visible and accessible names so the function remains recognizable.
<button type="submit">Search</button>

The criterion addresses components with the same functionality within a set of pages. Context can affect what a control does, so compare actual behavior as well as the icon. If two controls have different functions, making their names artificially identical may create a new problem.
Review and testing

Consistency does not mean unrelated controls must share a label or that every icon must look identical. Include accessible names in the review: two icons that look alike but have contradictory screen-reader names can still confuse users. Check surrounding context and function.
Names, icons and actual function

An icon and its accessible name may disagree. A magnifier announced as “Go” on one page and “Search” on another can make a repeated search feature harder to recognize. Inspect both the visible label and the computed accessible name. If an icon is accompanied by text, avoid introducing a conflicting aria-label that overrides that text.

A site can have more than one kind of search, such as searching lessons and searching support articles. Decide whether the controls truly have the same function before forcing identical labels. The criterion concerns consistency of identification across the relevant set of pages; matching colors or positioning alone do not establish it.
Recognizing the same function

A function is what a control or component does, not merely the shape of its icon. If a magnifying-glass button opens search on several pages, give it a consistent identification so a learner can recognize the same action. A familiar icon can supplement a label, but the accessible name must also communicate the function to someone who does not see the icon.

Review repeated controls across page templates, including mobile variants. Similar wording can be consistent even if grammar differs in context; conversely, identical-looking icons can be misleading when they perform different actions. Compare the control’s action, visible label, and accessible name together before deciding whether it is identified consistently.
Walkthrough: auditing repeated search controls

On one page a magnifying-glass button opens search and is named “Search”; on another, the same action is represented by the same icon but announced as “Find resources.” Compare the action, visible text, and accessible name across both pages. Decide whether the identification is understandable and consistent in context rather than judging the icon in isolation.

Fix a button that has no meaningful accessible name by providing an appropriate label. If visible text is also present, make sure its wording and the accessible name work together. A user who asks speech software to activate a visible control should not have to guess an unrelated programmatic name. Where the icon opens a different action on another page, use identification that distinguishes the functions.

Test the repeated component on all relevant templates, including the compact mobile navigation. Ask a learner to find the search action on a second page after learning it on the first. Inspect the accessibility tree and activate each control to verify what it actually does. Consistency of placement is related but belongs to a separate navigation requirement; a consistent label alone does not establish correct placement.
Apply the distinction

Compare a download action on a lesson page and a resource page. If both save the same kind of file, naming one “Download PDF” and the other only “Arrow” makes the second action harder to recognize, especially without the icon. Give repeated functionality identification that communicates the same purpose, including the accessible name. Conversely, if two similar icons have different outcomes, labels should distinguish those outcomes rather than forcing them to sound identical. Check translated versions as well as the original language; consistent identification concerns the function in context, not literal repetition of English words on every localized page.
Review a second case

Review case: A calendar icon opens a date picker on several forms, but one instance is announced as “Calendar,” another as “Choose date,” and a third has no accessible name. Inspect both what each button does and how it is identified. Use consistent, meaningful identification for the repeated date-selection function; preserve a visible label relationship where applicable. Then check a calendar icon that opens a schedule rather than a picker: because its function is different, an identical label could itself mislead. A consistent icon is helpful visual recognition, but it does not supply an accessible name on its own. Verify each instance in the accessibility tree, activate it, and check the result. This distinguishes consistent identification from merely giving every control with a similar picture the same text.
Implementation and verification

Compare components by their actual function before comparing names. Searching the course catalog and searching support articles can need different labels because the scopes differ. Identical search functions in repeated headers should be identified consistently. Inspect the computed accessible name and visible text: an aria-label can override visible wording and produce inconsistent announcements. Record the page, visible label, accessible name, and resulting action. Fix the shared component where possible, then retest each template with keyboard and screen reader. Consistent identification concerns function, not identical decoration.

Start at a realistic entry point and record the user's actions and resulting changes. Compare visible presentation with DOM order, keyboard route, accessible names, and any user preference relevant to the case. Test the default view and a narrow viewport when the same mechanism appears in both. Note whether the user initiated a change: an intentional selection and an unexpected transition create different experiences. Retest after modifying a shared component, since an older template may still exhibit the original problem. Record the specific pages, interaction steps, expected behavior, and actual behavior so another reviewer can reproduce the finding.
Knowledge check
How should the same search function be identified across pages? Consider the consequences of each approach before continuing.
Required practical activity

Inventory repeated search and help controls across a site. Compare visible labels, accessible names, and actual behavior; correct mismatches for equivalent functions. Record the barrier, the change you made, and the evidence from your test.
Key takeaway
Consistent identification helps readers recognize the same functionality. Consult the complete WCAG 2.2 criterion for its scope and exceptions.
Reference: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/

lessons.title: 3.2.5 Change on Request
lessons.objective: Ensure changes of context occur on request or can be disabled

content.text: Learning objectives
Ensure changes of context occur on request or can be disabled. This lesson addresses WCAG 2.2 3.2.5 Change on Request (Level AAA).
Why this matters

Unexpected changes in page, focus, or window can disrupt a task. At AAA, the criterion requires changes of context to be initiated by user request, or a mechanism to turn such changes off. This is broader than the specific focus and input situations addressed by related criteria.
How to apply the criterion

Use controls that make actions clear: open a new page when a user activates a link, and let the user choose whether automatic transitions occur. Where an automatic context change exists, provide a way to disable it. A clearly identified explicit action gives the user control.
Real-world example

An online tutorial automatically opens the next page after a timer. The learner may still be reading or may use a different reading pace. Replace the automatic transition with a Next button, or offer a mechanism to turn the automatic change off.
<button type="button" id="next-lesson">Next lesson</button>

A change of context is not the same as every update to a page. Assess whether the change substantially alters the user’s experience, such as a new page or a disruptive focus move. The AAA criterion applies to context changes generally, beyond the specific focus and input rules. Test automatic transitions after a page has been left open.
Review and testing

Do not confuse any small update with a change of context. Assess whether the change substantially affects the user’s interaction, such as moving focus, navigating, or changing the viewport. Test automatically timed flows as well as focus and input events.
Automatic transitions and user choice

A timed tutorial might open the next lesson automatically after a video. A learner who needs extra time may lose the current position. Give them control before the transition, for example by disabling automatic progression or choosing a Next action. If there is an on/off setting, make its current state and effect clear and allow it to be operated from the keyboard.

Check transitions caused by timers, focus, input, and background events. This criterion is broader than focus-only and input-only requirements, so a page can pass one of those and still need review here. Distinguish replacing a small piece of content from a change that alters the page, focus or other context in a substantial way.
Transitions initiated by the user

A change of context can include moving to a different page, opening a new window, or moving focus in a way that substantially changes the user’s interaction. A timed redirect after a lesson may remove the explanation before a reader is ready. Prefer a clearly labeled Next button, or provide a setting that lets the learner prevent an automatic transition.

Trace timers, background responses, focus handlers, and changes to form values. Ask whether a transition was initiated by the user or whether there was an accessible mechanism to turn it off. A small in-place update does not necessarily have the same effect as changing the page or focus; assess what the learner actually experiences.
Walkthrough: stopping automatic progression

A training page opens the next lesson ten seconds after a video ends. A learner who needs additional time to read the transcript may be moved before finishing. Provide an obvious Next action, or offer a control that lets the learner turn off automatic progression. Make the current setting clear and do not make the learner race a timer to find it.

Inspect other possible triggers as well. A redirect may be scheduled by a timer, fired by focus, caused by changing a select value, or initiated after a background request finishes. Trace what happens to the page, focus, and browser window. An in-place update of a small status message is not automatically equivalent to replacing the document; decide whether the change affects context in the relevant sense.

Test with automatic progression enabled and disabled. Confirm that disabling it persists for the promised scope, that the control works from the keyboard, and that the learner can still choose Next. Record which transition occurred, what initiated it, and whether the user had an accessible mechanism to prevent it. This enhanced criterion is broader than the focus-only and input-only requirements.
Apply the distinction

A timeout that moves the learner from a reading page to a survey may be triggered without deliberate action. Offer a way to prevent that transition before it happens, such as a clearly labeled automatic-advance setting, and verify that the setting controls the actual timer. If the user explicitly activates a Next link, record that user action as the trigger. A background refresh of a small score display is a different case from redirecting the browser or moving focus to another view; examine its actual effect. Test the disabled state for the duration promised and make sure the learner can still advance when ready.
Review a second case

Review case: A lesson displays a transcript and automatically moves to the next page five seconds after the video finishes. A learner who reads more slowly may lose the transcript before finishing. Provide an explicit Next control, or a mechanism to turn off the automatic change, and make that control available before the transition. Test whether the setting remains effective when the video ends and whether the user can advance manually afterward. A progress indicator that updates in place does not necessarily change context; the audit should observe whether the page, focus, or another significant context actually changes. Also inspect transitions from timers and background responses, not only those caused by focus or a changed form control. The question is whether the transition is user-initiated or an accessible turn-off mechanism exists.
Implementation and verification

A tutorial that advances automatically can remove context while a learner is still reading. Offer an accessible way to turn off automatic advancement or let the learner choose Next. Make the setting discoverable before the transition and expose its current state. Trace scripted focus movement, new windows, and background navigation as well. Ordinary content updates do not all qualify as context changes, so record the result and how it affects the user's interaction. Test that the chosen setting remains effective when the learner returns to the workflow.

Start at a realistic entry point and record the user's actions and resulting changes. Compare visible presentation with DOM order, keyboard route, accessible names, and any user preference relevant to the case. Test the default view and a narrow viewport when the same mechanism appears in both. Note whether the user initiated a change: an intentional selection and an unexpected transition create different experiences. Retest after modifying a shared component, since an older template may still exhibit the original problem. Record the specific pages, interaction steps, expected behavior, and actual behavior so another reviewer can reproduce the finding.
Knowledge check
How can an automatic context change meet this AAA requirement? Consider the consequences of each approach before continuing.
Required practical activity

Observe a multi-step interface for automatic redirects or focus changes. Document which changes are user initiated, and provide an accessible way to disable the others. Record the barrier, the change you made, and the evidence from your test.
Key takeaway
Users must initiate context changes or have a way to disable them. Consult the complete WCAG 2.2 criterion for its scope and exceptions.
Reference: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/

lessons.title: 3.2.6 Consistent Help
lessons.objective: Place repeated help mechanisms consistently

content.text: Learning objectives
Place repeated help mechanisms consistently. This lesson addresses WCAG 2.2 3.2.6 Consistent Help (Level A).
Why this matters

When people need assistance, predictability helps them find it quickly. A help link that moves from the header to an unrelated footer position on each page forces users to search again, especially when a task is already difficult.
How to apply the criterion

For applicable help mechanisms repeated across pages in a set, keep their relative order with respect to other page content consistent unless the user changes it. Examples include human contact details, a human contact mechanism, self-help information, and a fully automated contact mechanism.
Real-world example

A course site includes the same Help link in the header on several pages. Moving it between the header and footer makes it harder for a learner to find when stuck. Give the repeated help link a consistent relative position.
Courses Help

The rule applies to repeated help mechanisms of the specified types, such as contact details or self-help. It does not require an organization to add a help mechanism to every page. A user may initiate a change in relative order; document such customizations separately from the default layout.
Review and testing

The criterion applies when the same help mechanism is repeated; it does not require every page to add every kind of help. Compare positions across desktop and mobile pages and review source order as well as visual presentation.
Help across a set of pages

A learner may first find the support link while browsing a course and later need it when a form fails. Reusing the same position in the page structure helps them find it again. Record the help link relative to surrounding navigation, not merely whether a help icon exists somewhere on each page.

The criterion covers specified repeated help mechanisms, including human contact details or methods, self-help, and fully automated contact mechanisms. It does not demand the creation of a particular help service. A user-initiated change in order is allowed. Test repeated mechanisms across pages in the same set and inspect both mobile and desktop layouts.
Findable help across pages

A learner who encounters an error may remember that Help followed the course navigation. If the same contact method later appears before the logo or only inside an unrelated menu, finding it again takes extra effort. Keep repeated help mechanisms in a consistent relative order within the set of pages where they occur.

Compare the placement of the same support link, contact information, self-help option, or automated contact mechanism across representative pages. Responsive layouts can present the same order in different ways; check the actual reading and keyboard order as well. The criterion concerns the order of repeated mechanisms and does not, by itself, require a site to offer a particular type of help.
Walkthrough: comparing help locations

A course site shows a support link after the main navigation on the overview page. On the lesson and assessment pages, the same link appears before the logo. A learner who relies on a familiar sequence must search again at the moment they need help. Place repeated help mechanisms in a consistent relative order across the relevant pages, unless the learner has initiated a change.

Make an inventory of the repeated mechanisms: a contact link, a telephone number, a self-help page, or an automated contact method may each be relevant. Compare like with like. The rule does not require every page to invent a support option that the site never offered; it concerns the position of the specified mechanisms when they repeat.

Test the mobile menu and keyboard reading sequence as well as the desktop layout. Record the item immediately before and after the support mechanism on each representative page, then navigate to the help itself to make sure the link is usable. Consistent placement helps people locate support, but it does not guarantee that the support content will solve the underlying issue.
Apply the distinction

For an audit, choose a public course page, a lesson page, and an assessment page in the same set. If each repeats the same chat support and help-center links, write down their relative position to other repeated page components. A mobile menu can look different while still preserving a consistent sequence, but verify the order by opening it and navigating. If the user rearranges their own dashboard, record that as a user-initiated change. Avoid concluding that a page fails simply because it offers no additional contact method: the criterion focuses on relative order when the specified help mechanisms are repeated.
Review a second case

Review case: A site includes both a contact link and an automated support chat on its course, lesson, and assessment pages. On the assessment page the chat appears before the contact link, while on the other pages the order is reversed. Compare the repeated mechanisms in relation to each other and surrounding page elements, including in the mobile menu. Preserve a consistent relative sequence unless the user has chosen to change it. Test that the controls themselves work, but distinguish operational defects from this particular ordering requirement. A page that never offers a certain help mechanism does not automatically fail merely because the criterion mentions that kind of help; the requirement concerns relevant mechanisms that repeat within a set. Keep an audit record showing pages, viewport, and the order found.
Implementation and verification

Map repeated help mechanisms across a set of pages, such as a contact link, self-help route, or automated contact option. Compare their order relative to other content rather than merely checking that an icon exists. A Help link after the navigation on one page but before it on another can disrupt a learned route. Inspect the mobile layout and source order as well as the desktop presentation. The criterion does not require every page to introduce a help service. It allows user-initiated changes in order when applicable.

Start at a realistic entry point and record the user's actions and resulting changes. Compare visible presentation with DOM order, keyboard route, accessible names, and any user preference relevant to the case. Test the default view and a narrow viewport when the same mechanism appears in both. Note whether the user initiated a change: an intentional selection and an unexpected transition create different experiences. Retest after modifying a shared component, since an older template may still exhibit the original problem. Record the specific pages, interaction steps, expected behavior, and actual behavior so another reviewer can reproduce the finding.
Knowledge check
What does consistent help require when the same help link appears on several pages? Consider the consequences of each approach before continuing.
Required practical activity

Map the Help link and contact options across three pages. Check their relative placement and propose a consistent location that works at different viewport sizes. Record the barrier, the change you made, and the evidence from your test.
Key takeaway
The requirement concerns consistent placement of repeated applicable help mechanisms. Consult the complete WCAG 2.2 criterion for its scope and exceptions.
Reference: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/

lessons.title: 3.3.1 Error Identification
lessons.objective: Identify input errors in text

content.text: Learning objectives
Identify input errors in text. This lesson addresses WCAG 2.2 3.3.1 Error Identification (Level A).
Why this matters

A red border may be easy to miss and does not tell a screen-reader user what failed. An error needs to identify the problematic item and describe the error in text so that the person can understand what to fix.
How to apply the criterion

After validation, provide a clear message such as “Email address: enter an address in the form name@example.com.” Associate the message with the field, for example with aria-describedby, and communicate invalid state where appropriate. A summary can link to errors when a form is long.
Real-world example

A registration form detects a missing email and shows only a red border. Someone who cannot perceive the color receives no explanation. Add text that identifies the affected input and describes the problem.
Enter your email address.

Set the invalid state after a validation failure rather than labeling an untouched valid field as invalid. Make the error discoverable when it appears and preserve the user’s other entries. A field-specific message tells the user more than a generic alert; test the message association with the browser accessibility tree.
Review and testing

Do not rely only on color, an icon, or a generic “Invalid input” message detached from its field. Ensure the message describes the error without revealing sensitive information. Test server-side errors as well as client-side checks and verify messages remain visible when revisiting fields.
Communicating a failed submission

A form can show a summary near the top and a field-specific message near each invalid control. A summary helps users see the scope of the problem, while the local message helps them correct it. Link the summary to the relevant fields and make the association with each error available programmatically. Preserve entered values so correction does not become a new task.

Test missing, malformed, and server-rejected inputs. An error must identify the item and describe the problem in text; color or an unexplained icon alone is insufficient. Check how a dynamically inserted message is announced, where focus goes after submission, and whether the same message remains discoverable when the learner returns to the field.
Identifying the problem in context

An error message needs to tell the learner which item is affected and what went wrong in text. “Please enter an email address” identifies a missing value more clearly than turning an input border red. For several failures, a summary can name each item while local messages remain available next to the controls. Keep the text accurate when the server reports an error after submission.

Associate local error text with the relevant input and verify that a screen reader can discover it. Test an empty required field, an invalid format, and an error returned by the server. Confirm that the entered values remain available for correction and that the user can reach the affected field from the summary without hunting through the whole form.
Walkthrough: submitting an incomplete form

A learner submits a registration form without an email address and with an invalid date. A red outline alone does not tell someone who cannot perceive the color which input needs attention or why. Present text naming each error, such as “Enter an email address” and “Enter a valid date.” Keep messages near their controls and consider a summary that links to each affected field.

Associate the local message programmatically with the corresponding input and preserve the user’s other answers. When errors are added dynamically, test how they are announced and where focus goes; the learner should be able to discover the summary and return to the field. A summary does not replace the need for an intelligible message when the learner reaches the input.

Correct one field and submit again. Verify that the fixed error disappears or updates, the remaining error is still accurate, and no unrelated input was erased. Test a server-rejected value as well as client-side checks. Error identification explains what went wrong; the separate error-suggestion requirement concerns suitable advice on how to fix it when such advice is known and safe.
Apply the distinction

A useful error summary might say “There are two errors: Email address: enter a value; Date: enter a valid date.” Each link can move the learner to the relevant field. Test that the individual field also has the corresponding message and that the summary does not become stale after one error is corrected. Keep the text distinct from a general server outage message, which should not falsely blame a particular input. A red border or warning icon may reinforce the message visually, but color or shape alone cannot identify both the affected item and the problem in text. Preserve previously entered values during correction.
Review a second case

Review case: A form accepts an email address locally but the server rejects it because it is already registered. Display a text message that identifies the affected email field and describes the problem, provided the disclosure is appropriate for the application’s security context. Associate the message with the field and preserve the rest of the learner’s input. If a summary appears, make it possible to reach the problematic field and ensure the same message remains available there. A color change or an icon can reinforce the error but cannot replace its textual identification. Test after correcting the value: remove or update the obsolete message, and confirm a screen reader user can find the current state. In a security-sensitive flow, choose wording that identifies the problem without unnecessarily revealing account information.
Implementation and verification

After submitting an invalid form, review both the error summary and each affected field. A summary can link to errors while local messages identify each problem in text. Preserve entered values so a person can correct a mistake without starting over. Check server-reported errors as well as browser validation, since they may follow a different rendering path. Verify that messages remain discoverable when focus returns to fields and that a colored outline is not the sole cue. A generic “invalid” message may leave users guessing which item and problem need attention.

Follow the learner from the initial instructions through submission, recovery, and final confirmation. Try a realistic mistake, record the message and focus behavior, correct it, and verify the final data. Test the server response as well, because browser validation cannot cover every rejection. Use representative test values that do not expose real personal or financial information in the evidence. Review the experience using keyboard and, where relevant, a screen reader. Keep instructions, validation logic, and help aligned whenever a form or policy changes. Record the route tested and the resulting behavior so the team can reproduce the issue.
Knowledge check
Which error response identifies the problem in text? Consider the consequences of each approach before continuing.
Required practical activity

Submit a form with a missing email address. Add a text error, connect it to the field, and verify the field and message with keyboard and a screen reader. Record the barrier, the change you made, and the evidence from your test.
Key takeaway
A text description identifies both the affected item and its error. Consult the complete WCAG 2.2 criterion for its scope and exceptions.

lessons.title: 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions
lessons.objective: Provide labels or instructions for inputs

content.text: Learning objectives
Provide labels or instructions for inputs. This lesson addresses WCAG 2.2 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions (Level A).
Why this matters

People need to know what information a field expects before making an error. A placeholder that disappears on typing can remove the only visible instruction and leave readers uncertain about the field’s purpose.
How to apply the criterion

Give each input a meaningful label and provide instructions where required, such as the expected date format or mandatory fields. In HTML, connect a label using for and id, and associate supporting text with aria-describedby when appropriate. Group related radio buttons with fieldset and legend.
Real-world example

A date field displays only “MM/DD/YYYY” as a placeholder. Once the user types, that text disappears, and they can no longer see whether the field asks for a birthday or an appointment date. A persistent label and visible instruction solve different parts of the problem.
Use MM/DD/YYYY.

A label names the field; instructions describe additional expectations such as the format. Provide both when necessary. An accessible name that exists only in hidden text may help a screen-reader user but leave a sighted user without a visible instruction. Validate with real users and keyboard input.
Review and testing

A programmatic accessible name and visible instructions are related but distinct concerns. A screen-reader-only name does not necessarily help a sighted person who cannot infer a field’s purpose. Avoid placing essential format rules solely in an error after submission.
Labels, instructions and grouping

A label answers “What is this input?” Instructions answer “What details do I need to provide?” For a telephone field, a visible label can identify the field and nearby text can explain whether a country code is required. Instructions should match the actual accepted formats and remain available after typing begins.

For a set of related options, use a group label as well as individual option labels. Native fieldset and legend are useful for related radio buttons and checkboxes. Test the complete accessible name and associated description; a placeholder, color-coded asterisk, or icon alone may not explain requirements to every learner.
Labels and instructions serve different purposes

A visible label tells the learner what information a control collects. Instructions explain additional conditions, such as a required format, a range, or whether the field is mandatory. For example, “Date of birth” names the field; “Use day/month/year” explains how to enter the value. Place the instruction where it remains available when the user begins typing.

A placeholder is not a dependable replacement for a label because it disappears or becomes harder to see as text is entered. Programmatically associate the label and relevant instructions with the field, and use a fieldset and legend when a group of related choices needs a shared question. Test both visible presentation and the name and description announced for the input.
Walkthrough: building a date field

Give the input a visible label such as “Appointment date” and associate that label with the control. Explain the accepted format before entry, for example “Use day/month/year, such as 25/04/2026,” when the implementation actually expects that format. If the date is required, communicate that in text or another accessible manner rather than relying on an unexplained colored symbol.

A placeholder can illustrate a format, but it may disappear as the user types and does not reliably replace a persistent label or instruction. Connect supporting instructions to the input programmatically and check the accessible name and description. For a group of radio buttons, use a group question and individual option labels so that each choice makes sense when encountered independently.

Test the form without a mouse and with a screen reader. Before entering anything, can the learner identify the field, determine the expected value, and understand whether it is mandatory? Enter a valid example and verify that the application accepts exactly what the instructions promise. Revisit the guidance whenever validation changes.
Apply the distinction

A shipping form may ask for an address, a postal code, and a country. Make clear which fields are required and provide format guidance only where it applies; a rigid example that is valid for one country may mislead someone using another. Associate each label with its input rather than relying solely on visual proximity. For related checkboxes, a fieldset and legend can provide the shared question while each checkbox retains its own label. Inspect the browser accessibility tree and tab through the form: the learner should hear enough information before entering a value and should not need to erase a placeholder to find the expected format.
Review a second case

Review case: A date field has the placeholder “MM/DD/YYYY” but no visible label. Once a learner starts typing, the placeholder disappears, leaving no persistent indication of what the date represents or what format is expected. Add a visible label identifying the date and separate instructions describing the format accepted by the application. Associate both with the control programmatically, and communicate if the value is required. If the product accepts multiple formats, do not falsely state that only one is permitted. Test a screen reader’s announced name and description, then enter a value to check that the guidance remains available. A fieldset and legend are useful when several controls answer one shared question, but individual controls still need understandable labels.
Implementation and verification

Base instructions on values the system actually accepts. If a date field accepts a specific format, provide it and an example before entry. Keep the visible label available after typing begins; placeholder text alone disappears. Associate the supporting description with the field and use a group label for related choices. Test at increased zoom and inspect the accessibility tree. Ask a new learner what information the field expects before submitting it. When requirements depend on an earlier choice, update the instructions accordingly and explain required indicators without relying only on color.

Follow the learner from the initial instructions through submission, recovery, and final confirmation. Try a realistic mistake, record the message and focus behavior, correct it, and verify the final data. Test the server response as well, because browser validation cannot cover every rejection. Use representative test values that do not expose real personal or financial information in the evidence. Review the experience using keyboard and, where relevant, a screen reader. Keep instructions, validation logic, and help aligned whenever a form or policy changes. Record the route tested and the resulting behavior so the team can reproduce the issue.
Knowledge check
Which design helps users know what to enter before an error? Consider the consequences of each approach before continuing.
Required practical activity

Create a date field with a visible label and format guidance. Verify the association in the accessibility tree and ask a new user to complete the field before seeing any error. Record the barrier, the change you made, and the evidence from your test.
Key takeaway
Labels and instructions tell users what the input expects. Consult the complete WCAG 2.2 criterion for its scope and exceptions.
Reference: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/

lessons.title: 3.3.3 Error Suggestion
lessons.objective: Suggest corrections when known and appropriate

content.text: Learning objectives
Suggest corrections when known and appropriate. This lesson addresses WCAG 2.2 3.3.3 Error Suggestion (Level AA).
Why this matters
Knowing that an entry is invalid is useful; knowing how to correct it makes recovery much easier. A generic rejection may force users to guess a format or repeat the same failure.
How to apply the criterion

When an input error is detected and a correction suggestion is known, provide it unless doing so would jeopardize security or the purpose of the content. For example, “Enter the date as DD/MM/YYYY” supplies actionable guidance when the format is known.
Real-world example

A user enters a date in the wrong format and sees only “Invalid”. The system knows which format it accepts, so it can give a useful, safe suggestion. Place that guidance with the identified field and retain the entered value for correction.
Enter the date as MM/DD/YYYY, for example 03/15/2026.

Do not provide a correction if doing so compromises security or the content’s purpose. For example, a sign-in failure should not reveal confidential account information. Suggestions complement error identification: the user still needs to know which input is affected and be able to correct it.
Review and testing

Do not expose a secret or confirm account existence merely to provide a suggestion. Error identification and error suggestion work together: identify the field, describe what went wrong, and provide safe guidance. Ensure a suggestion does not silently overwrite a user’s entry.
Actionable and safe correction

A suggestion should tell the user what to do next, not merely restate that the value is wrong. For a date with a known expected format, offer the format and a realistic example. For a value outside an accepted range, provide the range when it is safe to do so. Keep the original value available so the user can edit it.

Security and purpose matter. A sign-in message that distinguishes an unknown account from a wrong password may reveal information an attacker can use; a general credential message may be appropriate. This criterion applies when a suggestion is known, unless disclosure would jeopardize security or the purpose of the content. Pair it with clear error identification.
Suggestions that match the actual rule

If a date is rejected because the application expects a particular format, an error such as “Enter a date as DD/MM/YYYY, for example 25/04/2026” helps the user repair it. If the system knows that a number is outside an accepted range, a safe message can explain that range. Retain the value already entered so the learner can correct it instead of starting again.

Do not reveal information that would compromise security or the purpose of the content. For example, a login error may need to avoid confirming whether a particular account exists. Check that every suggestion matches the current validation rules and that it is associated with the field. A useful suggestion complements, rather than replaces, identifying the error itself.
Walkthrough: repairing a rejected date

A form displays “Invalid input” after a learner enters 31/02/2026. The message signals a failure but does not explain how to proceed. If the application can tell that the date is impossible, explain that the day must exist in the chosen month and give a valid example. If the issue is the expected format, provide the format that the validation actually accepts.

Keep the entered value and make the suggestion available near the input. Programmatically associate it with the field so a learner returning to the control can find it. Test both an impossible date and a valid date in the wrong format: one generic suggestion may not help both cases. After a correction, ensure the message no longer contradicts the current value.

The criterion applies when a correction is known, unless providing it would jeopardize security or the purpose of the content. A login system may give a general credential error rather than revealing whether an account exists. Document why a suggestion is withheld where applicable, and check that an accessible error identification is still present.
Apply the distinction

Compare two messages for a quantity field: “Invalid” and “Enter a whole number from 1 to 10.” The second suggests a correction when the range is known and disclosure is safe. Test a non-number and a number outside the range, and confirm the advice is accurate for both. Retain the original input and let the learner edit it; automatically replacing it with a guessed value can conceal an unintended choice. For authentication, revealing which part of the credentials was wrong can create security concerns, so a general message may be appropriate. Error identification and a safe, known correction suggestion work together but answer different questions.
Review a second case

Review case: A registration form says “Password invalid” although it knows that the password must contain at least twelve characters. When disclosure is safe, explain the requirement and retain the user’s input so it can be corrected. Test too-short input and a valid input, and ensure the guidance agrees with server-side validation. Do not expose a user’s secret in an error summary or provide suggestions that compromise security. A general sign-in error may be appropriate when specifying whether the account or password was wrong would reveal sensitive information. Separate the question “Which item has an error?” from “What known change would fix it?”; both may need to be addressed. Check that the learner can find the relevant message when returning to the field.
Implementation and verification

For a value outside a known permitted range, name the range when disclosure is safe and keep the entry available for correction. The advice must reflect the actual validation rule; stale help can cause repeated failure. For sign-in, a precise suggestion may reveal whether an account exists, so consider the security exception. Test messages after client-side and server-side rejection and ensure that the suggestion accompanies the detected error. Identifying an error and suggesting how to correct it are related but distinct tasks; a message should support both when the conditions apply.

Follow the learner from the initial instructions through submission, recovery, and final confirmation. Try a realistic mistake, record the message and focus behavior, correct it, and verify the final data. Test the server response as well, because browser validation cannot cover every rejection. Use representative test values that do not expose real personal or financial information in the evidence. Review the experience using keyboard and, where relevant, a screen reader. Keep instructions, validation logic, and help aligned whenever a form or policy changes. Record the route tested and the resulting behavior so the team can reproduce the issue.
Knowledge check
When a known date format is entered incorrectly, what is a useful response? Consider the consequences of each approach before continuing.
Required practical activity

Test a date field with an invalid format and a sign-in form with an invalid credential. Write helpful, safe messages for each without exposing sensitive information. Record the barrier, the change you made, and the evidence from your test.
Key takeaway
A known safe correction helps the user recover. Consult the complete WCAG 2.2 criterion for its scope and exceptions.
Reference: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/

lessons.title: 3.3.4 Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data)
lessons.objective: Protect important legal, financial, and data submissions from errors

content.text: Learning objectives
Protect important legal, financial, and data submissions from errors. This lesson addresses WCAG 2.2 3.3.4 Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data) (Level AA).
Why this matters

An accidental financial transfer, legal acceptance, or modification of stored data can have serious consequences. Users may misread an amount, activate the wrong control, or submit before noticing an error. Recovery needs to be designed into the workflow.
How to apply the criterion

For the covered submissions, provide at least one of the specified safeguards: the submission is reversible, entered data is checked for errors with a chance to correct them, or a review, confirmation, and correction mechanism is available before finalizing. The exact scope and exceptions should be read in the complete criterion.
Real-world example

A learner pays a course fee and accidentally chooses the wrong recipient. A review step can present the recipient and amount and allow correction before committing the payment. The user should be able to go back without losing the entire form.

Review payment

Recipient: Course office

Amount: 500 pesos

Edit payment

The criterion permits a covered submission to be reversible, checked for errors with a chance to correct, or reviewed, confirmed, and corrected before final submission. A vague “Are you sure?” dialog is weak if it gives no way to inspect or correct the details. Check the full criterion for covered legal commitments, financial transactions, user-controlled data, and test responses.
Review and testing

A confirmation screen that merely says “Are you sure?” without showing details does not help a user review the amount or recipient. Display meaningful values and allow editing before final action. Clearly distinguish saving a draft from committing a transaction.
Selecting and testing a safeguard

A reversible transaction requires a practical way to reverse the result, not just a promise that support might help. An input-checking approach must identify detected errors and let the user correct them. A review approach must show meaningful data before final submission, allow corrections, and clearly distinguish the final confirmation action from editing.

Walk through a test payment with a deliberately incorrect amount. Verify the learner can notice and correct it before commitment or use the chosen safeguard afterward. The criterion covers specified legal, financial, user-controlled data and test-response situations; verify the full scope and any exceptions rather than assuming it applies identically to all forms.
Comparing prevention mechanisms

For a payment, a review step can show the amount, recipient, and other consequential values before final confirmation. A learner must be able to return and correct a mistake without losing unrelated information. Alternatively, a genuinely reversible operation or checks that identify errors and allow correction can provide one of the criterion’s specified safeguards.

Test the safeguard with a deliberately wrong value. A generic “Are you sure?” prompt that does not show what will be submitted may not give the learner a useful opportunity to review. If relying on reversal, verify that it actually restores the prior state; if relying on input checking, verify that a detected error can be corrected before the transaction is committed.
Walkthrough: reviewing a financial submission

A learner is about to pay a course fee. The review screen displays the amount, recipient, and chosen payment method, with a way to edit each before a final confirmation button. Enter an incorrect amount deliberately, continue to review, and correct it. Confirm that returning to edit does not remove other entries and that the corrected value appears on the final review.

The criterion allows specified alternatives: a submission may be reversible, input may be checked for errors with an opportunity to correct them, or the user may review, confirm, and correct before finalizing. Evaluate the mechanism actually provided. A confirmation dialog that only asks “Continue?” without revealing the important values may not enable meaningful review.

If reversal is claimed, test the real reversal path and any time limit; a vague instruction to contact support is not evidence that reversal works. If error checking is used, test an error that the application is capable of detecting. Identify whether the transaction falls in the criterion’s covered legal, financial, user-controlled data, or test-response situations, and document the specific safeguard observed.
Apply the distinction

Suppose a form deletes user-controlled data after a confirmation step. A review mechanism should show which data is affected and offer a way to cancel or correct the selection. A generic OK button does not establish what will be lost. Alternatively, if deletion is reversible, verify that a restoration path really restores the data and make any meaningful limitation clear. If input checking is the selected safeguard, demonstrate a detectable error and an opportunity to fix it. Test the actual submission path, not just the presence of an extra screen. The applicable scope and the chosen safeguard determine what evidence a reviewer needs.
Review a second case

Review case: A learner submits an assessment whose response is final. Before confirmation, show the answers and allow the learner to return to an item and change it. Deliberately change one response during review and verify the final submitted answer reflects that change. If the application claims reversibility instead, test whether a submitted response can actually be withdrawn or corrected; a visual Undo control that leaves the stored result unchanged is not an effective safeguard. If relying on checking, identify which errors the system detects and confirm a user can correct them. The requirement covers specified high-consequence categories, so determine whether the interaction falls within its scope and record the safeguard used rather than assuming every form must have a review page.
Implementation and verification

Trace the transaction from entry to final commitment. For an applicable legal or financial submission, determine whether the safeguard is reversal, checking with a correction opportunity, or review and confirmation. A review screen must show meaningful details, allow edits, and submit corrected values rather than stale data. If reversal is the safeguard, verify that it can actually be performed and the outcome communicated. If checking is used, introduce a detectable error and confirm the user can correct it. Check the full scope of the criterion when selecting and evaluating the safeguard.

Follow the learner from the initial instructions through submission, recovery, and final confirmation. Try a realistic mistake, record the message and focus behavior, correct it, and verify the final data. Test the server response as well, because browser validation cannot cover every rejection. Use representative test values that do not expose real personal or financial information in the evidence. Review the experience using keyboard and, where relevant, a screen reader. Keep instructions, validation logic, and help aligned whenever a form or policy changes. Record the route tested and the resulting behavior so the team can reproduce the issue.
Knowledge check
Which safeguard can protect an important financial submission? Consider the consequences of each approach before continuing.
Required practical activity

Design a transfer review page that shows recipient and amount and lets the user change either before confirming. Test with keyboard and explain how the safeguard prevents an error. Record the barrier, the change you made, and the evidence from your test.
Key takeaway
A review and correction step is one of the permitted safeguards. Consult the complete WCAG 2.2 criterion for its scope and exceptions.
Reference: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/

lessons.title: 3.3.5 Help
lessons.objective: Offer context-sensitive help

content.text: Learning objectives
Offer context-sensitive help. This lesson addresses WCAG 2.2 3.3.5 Help (Level AAA).
Why this matters

General documentation can be useful, but someone filling a specific field often needs an explanation of that field at the moment of entry. Context-sensitive help relates to the current task or control rather than requiring the user to search an unrelated manual.
How to apply the criterion

Place an explanation next to an input or link to help that opens at the relevant topic. For an account name, explain restrictions and give an example. Make the help available to keyboard, touch, and assistive-technology users without removing their work.
Real-world example
A learner filling a username field does not know which characters are accepted. Context-sensitive help placed beside the field can answer that question before submission and reduce trial and error.
Use 3–20 letters or numbers.

The example is an instructional pattern; actual restrictions must match server validation. A more complex explanation may use a help link or dialog if it remains keyboard accessible and does not discard the form. Context-sensitive help differs from a broad support page because it addresses the user’s immediate input or task.
Review and testing

Do not hide the only help in a hover-only tooltip. Consider whether opening a help dialog moves focus predictably and whether closing it returns focus to the initiating control. Help is different from an error message: it supports the user before or during input.
Making help available at the point of need

Help can be directly visible, linked from the control, or provided through another accessible mechanism. Inline help reduces navigation, but a long explanation may work better in a linked section or dialog. In either case, describe the specific information needed for the current field and provide an example consistent with validation rules.

Test that opening help does not clear the form. If a dialog opens, focus should enter it, the help should be readable, and closing it should return the user to a sensible location. Do not rely on a mouse-only hover effect. Validate the text after requirements change so it does not instruct users to enter a value the application rejects.
Help tailored to the task

Context-sensitive help answers a question the learner is likely to have at a particular point. Near an account-name field, explain the accepted characters and give a valid example. A general help home page may contain the answer, but it forces the learner to search and infer which article applies. Keep concise guidance near the field and link to longer explanations when needed.

If help opens in a dialog, verify that it is keyboard operable, its contents are announced, and closing it returns focus to a sensible location. Opening or closing help should not discard entered values. After validation rules change, update examples and help text together; instructions that suggest an invalid value can create the very error they should prevent.
Walkthrough: help for a username field

A registration form rejects a username but the learner cannot tell which characters are allowed. Add concise guidance adjacent to the field, such as the real permitted length and character rules. If the policy is complex, link to a detailed explanation with a clear name while retaining the most important rules next to the input.

Test the help before entering a value and after an error. A keyboard user should be able to reach any help link, read its content, and return to the form without losing their work. If help opens as a dialog, check that focus moves into it, the contents are readable, and closing it returns the learner to a sensible location. Avoid relying on a hover-only icon.

Compare every example with the actual server validation. A sample containing a character that the backend rejects undermines the help even if the help is technically reachable. Ask someone unfamiliar with the form to choose a valid username using only the available instructions. Context-sensitive help addresses the current task; a generic support page with no guidance for the field may leave the learner searching.
Apply the distinction

For an address field, help might explain where to find an apartment number and whether it belongs on a separate line. A help page about all account settings may be useful generally but require the learner to search for this specific answer. Link to the precise relevant section and keep critical guidance visible where possible. Test at a narrow viewport, with keyboard focus and with text zoomed, to make sure the help is reachable and does not cover the form permanently. After returning from help, verify the earlier form entries remain intact. Update the help when backend rules or accepted address formats change.
Review a second case

Review case: A form asks for a student identifier but learners do not know where to find it. Provide field-specific help such as the location on an enrollment notice and an example that matches the expected format, without displaying real personal identifiers. Place a concise explanation near the field and link to fuller guidance if necessary. Test opening that guidance with the keyboard, reading it at increased zoom, and returning without losing the value already entered. If a dialog is used, check focus entry, an accessible close control, and a sensible return point. Verify examples against validation rules when the identifier format changes. Context-sensitive help should answer the problem at this step; sending users to an unrelated general support page can leave the key question unanswered.
Implementation and verification

Help should answer a question relevant to the current task. A tax identifier field might need to explain where to find the number and show the accepted format. Longer help can be linked from the field to an accessible section or dialog; opening it should not erase entered values. Test opening, reading, closing, and returning with keyboard and screen reader. Keep the guidance aligned with validation rules. A generic support page can be useful, but check whether it actually provides the context-sensitive information needed for this field.

Follow the learner from the initial instructions through submission, recovery, and final confirmation. Try a realistic mistake, record the message and focus behavior, correct it, and verify the final data. Test the server response as well, because browser validation cannot cover every rejection. Use representative test values that do not expose real personal or financial information in the evidence. Review the experience using keyboard and, where relevant, a screen reader. Keep instructions, validation logic, and help aligned whenever a form or policy changes. Record the route tested and the resulting behavior so the team can reproduce the issue.
Knowledge check
Which is an example of context-sensitive help? Consider the consequences of each approach before continuing.
Required practical activity

Add contextual help to a password field and verify that a keyboard user can open, read, and leave the help while retaining entered data. Record the barrier, the change you made, and the evidence from your test.
Key takeaway
The help addresses the user’s current context. Consult the complete WCAG 2.2 criterion for its scope and exceptions.
Reference: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/

lessons.title: 3.3.6 Error Prevention (All)
lessons.objective: Apply error-prevention safeguards to all user submissions

content.text: Learning objectives
Apply error-prevention safeguards to all user submissions. This lesson addresses WCAG 2.2 3.3.6 Error Prevention (All) (Level AAA).
Why this matters

A small form submission can still have consequences for a person who made a mistake. The AAA criterion extends the error-prevention choices to submissions involving user input beyond the important categories covered by the AA criterion.
How to apply the criterion

Provide at least one of the allowed approaches: reversibility, input checking with an opportunity to correct errors, or a mechanism to review, confirm, and correct information before final submission. Choose a safeguard appropriate to the action rather than adding a meaningless confirmation dialog.
Real-world example

A learner changes a public profile description and submits the wrong text. An Undo action that restores the previous description can protect the submission. A review-and-correct step or relevant input checks with correction are other approaches.
Profile saved.

The button is only an illustration: application code must actually restore the previous value, communicate whether the undo succeeded, and make the action available long enough to use. The enhanced criterion extends the safeguards to submissions of information by the user more generally; a decorative confirmation button alone is not a safeguard.
Review and testing

A reversible action needs an effective way to undo it. A validation check should catch relevant errors and let the user fix them; it should not silently discard input. A review page must let a user correct details before committing the submission.
Safeguards for ordinary submissions

Consider a learner updating a profile. Undo is convenient when it is reliable and discoverable; review can be preferable where changes have visible consequences; input checking is useful when the system can identify errors. Each approach has different implementation and testing costs. Select one of the specified safeguards and verify it works for the submission.

If an Undo control appears, test restoring the earlier value and communicating success or failure. If validation is the safeguard, submit a detectable error and verify a correction opportunity. If review is used, change a value at review and ensure the final submission includes the corrected data. The enhanced criterion covers user submissions more broadly than the AA criterion.
Useful safeguards for routine changes

A profile form may not involve payment, but accidentally changing a setting can still be disruptive. A review step allows the learner to inspect values before saving; validation can identify a detectable input error and offer correction; a reliable Undo can reverse the change afterward. The criterion provides these approaches as alternatives, so select a mechanism that makes sense for the submission.

Run a realistic scenario rather than checking that an Undo label exists. Change a setting, save it, use Undo, and confirm that the old value is restored. For a review mechanism, edit a value from the review screen and verify that the final saved record contains the correction. Document limitations so a user is not promised a reversal that the system cannot perform.
Walkthrough: safeguarding a profile change

A learner changes a profile setting and presses Save. Choose a safeguard appropriate to the action: allow a reliable Undo, check for detectable input errors and allow corrections, or offer a review and confirmation step. A routine form may not be covered by the narrower categories of the related AA criterion, but this enhanced criterion extends safeguards to submissions involving user input.

If Undo is used, make it discoverable and test its actual effect. Change the value, save it, activate Undo, refresh the page, and verify that the previous value was restored. If the restoration fails, communicate that failure instead of reporting success. A visual change that is not persisted is not a reliable reversal.

For validation, submit a detectable invalid value and verify that it can be corrected. For a review step, change a value during review and verify that the final submitted data contains the correction. Do not add a meaningless confirmation screen merely to create an extra click; the learner needs a practical opportunity to prevent or repair a mistake.
Apply the distinction

A review screen can support a profile update by showing the proposed values and providing an Edit action before Save. Verify that the learner can change one field without losing the rest, and that the final submission uses the revised value. If a system instead provides Undo, check the saved state after the reversal and a refresh. If relying on input checking, ensure a detected error produces a chance to correct it rather than silently rejecting or discarding the submission. The enhanced criterion applies the specified prevention mechanisms more broadly than the related AA criterion; it does not prescribe the same design for every form.
Review a second case

Review case: A learner submits a profile biography and later notices an accidental edit. If the product offers Undo as its safeguard, save a change, invoke Undo, refresh the page, and verify the previously stored biography is restored. If the product uses a review-and-confirm path instead, edit the biography from review and verify that the final record contains the corrected text. If relying on checking, demonstrate a detectable error and an opportunity to fix it. The user should receive clear feedback when an operation succeeds or fails. This enhanced criterion applies to user submissions more broadly than the high-consequence situations of the related minimum criterion, but the chosen safeguard must still provide a practical correction opportunity rather than a decorative confirmation.
Implementation and verification

Apply the enhanced safeguard to the broader set of submissions covered by this criterion, including an ordinary profile update. Test the selected safeguard end to end. For reversal, change a value, undo it, and verify the original returns. For checking, introduce a detectable mistake and correct it. For review, confirm the summary includes the values, provides an edit route, and submits those edits. A warning with no usable action is not a working safeguard. Compare this broader coverage with the more limited situations in the related AA criterion.

Follow the learner from the initial instructions through submission, recovery, and final confirmation. Try a realistic mistake, record the message and focus behavior, correct it, and verify the final data. Test the server response as well, because browser validation cannot cover every rejection. Use representative test values that do not expose real personal or financial information in the evidence. Review the experience using keyboard and, where relevant, a screen reader. Keep instructions, validation logic, and help aligned whenever a form or policy changes. Record the route tested and the resulting behavior so the team can reproduce the issue.
Knowledge check
How does the AAA error-prevention criterion differ from the AA criterion? Consider the consequences of each approach before continuing.
Required practical activity

Pick an ordinary profile update. Add an effective undo, validation and correction, or review-and-confirm path, then test a deliberately incorrect value. Record the barrier, the change you made, and the evidence from your test.
Key takeaway
The enhanced criterion extends protection beyond the categories in the AA criterion. Consult the complete WCAG 2.2 criterion for its scope and exceptions.
Reference: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/

lessons.title: 3.3.7 Redundant Entry
lessons.objective: Avoid asking users to re-enter information in the same process

content.text: Learning objectives
Avoid asking users to re-enter information in the same process. This lesson addresses WCAG 2.2 3.3.7 Redundant Entry (Level A).
Why this matters
Repeatedly entering the same address or other information can be difficult for people with memory, motor, or cognitive disabilities. It can also introduce inconsistencies in a multi-step process.
How to apply the criterion

When information previously entered by or provided to the user is needed again in the same process, auto-populate it or make it available for selection. For example, offer the previously entered shipping address as a selectable billing address. The user should be able to inspect and change it when appropriate.
Real-world example

A checkout asks for a shipping address on the first step and the same address again on the payment step. Offer the previous address as a selectable billing address, while still allowing a different one.
<label><input type="checkbox" name="same-address"> Use my shipping address for billing</label>

The application must retain and apply the earlier information when the user selects it; the checkbox by itself does not perform that work. Exceptions cover cases where re-entry is essential, necessary for security, or the earlier information is no longer valid. Check that the selection remains editable and that stored personal information is handled appropriately.
Review and testing

The criterion includes exceptions when re-entry is essential, needed for security, or the previously entered information is no longer valid. It does not prohibit an optional alternative address. Distinguish a genuinely new process from steps within a single process, and protect sensitive data appropriately.
Same-process reuse and exceptions

In a checkout, a customer may need a billing address that differs from shipping. Reuse should therefore be an offered choice or editable prefilled value, not a forced assumption that both addresses are identical. Make it clear what information was carried forward and provide an easy way to correct it.

The rule concerns previously entered or supplied information needed again in the same process. Re-entry can still be necessary when it is essential, required for security, or the previous information is no longer valid. Evaluate the reason rather than treating every repeat field as automatically forbidden. Verify the selected value reaches the final submission correctly.
Reuse without forcing an incorrect value

A checkout may collect a delivery address and later ask for billing information. Offer the delivery address as a selectable option or prefill the repeated information, while letting a learner enter a different billing address. Reuse is valuable because it reduces memory and typing demands, but the learner should be able to see what was carried forward and correct it.

Check the entire process, including moving backward and forward between steps. Confirm that reused data reaches the final submission and that edits do not overwrite the original address unexpectedly. Re-entry is permitted under the criterion’s specified exceptions, including essential re-entry, security, or information that is no longer valid; record the actual reason rather than assuming repetition is always required.
Walkthrough: shipping and billing details

A checkout asks for a shipping address, then requests a billing address in a later step of the same process. Offer “Use shipping address” as a selectable option or prefill the previously supplied information. Show the carried-forward value so the learner can inspect it. If billing is different, make changing the value straightforward instead of forcing both addresses to match.

Test three paths: reuse the existing address unchanged, edit a copied address, and enter a different address. Move back and forward through the steps and check that the final order contains the chosen values. Pay particular attention to whether editing the billing address accidentally changes the original shipping address.

Review the criterion’s exceptions before concluding that re-entry is a failure. Re-entry can be essential, required for security, or justified because the previous information is no longer valid. These are reasons to evaluate in the actual process, not a blanket reason to require repeated typing everywhere. Protect sensitive information when displaying a reused value and distinguish a new process from steps in the same one.
Apply the distinction

An address offered for reuse may later become invalid because the learner changed it or it was supplied in an earlier, separate process. Review whether the previously provided information is still valid and whether the request belongs to the same process. When reuse is appropriate, present an editable choice and show what will be submitted. Test a person who needs a separate billing address; the interface must not silently force the delivery address into the billing record. Security can justify re-entry in some circumstances, but record why that specific information must be entered again rather than using a generic security claim for every field.
Review a second case

Review case: A learner enters an email address at the start of an application and is asked for the same address again during a later step. Offer the existing address for selection or populate it, then allow an alternative address if the task requires one. Verify the final application contains the learner’s selected value and that navigating backward does not unexpectedly replace it. Consider whether the request is within the same process and whether previous information remains valid. The criterion provides exceptions for essential re-entry, security, and information that is no longer valid; evaluate the actual reason for this field instead of applying an unsupported blanket exception. Showing the reused value helps a learner catch a typo, but avoid exposing sensitive information to an unintended person.
Implementation and verification

Follow a single process and record the information already supplied. When the process needs it again, offer an editable prefilled value or a selection of the earlier value. For example, offer a shipping address for billing without forcing the two addresses to match. Verify that the chosen or edited value reaches final submission. Re-entry can be justified when it is essential, necessary for security, or earlier information is no longer valid; record the actual reason. This criterion concerns information needed again within the same process, not automatically every earlier visit.

Follow the learner from the initial instructions through submission, recovery, and final confirmation. Try a realistic mistake, record the message and focus behavior, correct it, and verify the final data. Test the server response as well, because browser validation cannot cover every rejection. Use representative test values that do not expose real personal or financial information in the evidence. Review the experience using keyboard and, where relevant, a screen reader. Keep instructions, validation logic, and help aligned whenever a form or policy changes. Record the route tested and the resulting behavior so the team can reproduce the issue.
Knowledge check
How can a checkout avoid redundant entry? Consider the consequences of each approach before continuing.
Required practical activity

Build a checkout flow that offers the shipping address for billing. Test accepting it, editing it, and choosing a different address without retyping unnecessarily. Record the barrier, the change you made, and the evidence from your test.
Key takeaway
Making previously supplied information selectable avoids unnecessary re-entry. Consult the complete WCAG 2.2 criterion for its scope and exceptions.
Reference: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/
