lessons.title: 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum)
lessons.objective: Provide accessible authentication without mandatory cognitive-function tests

content.text: Learning objectives
Provide accessible authentication without mandatory cognitive-function tests. This lesson addresses WCAG 2.2 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) (Level AA).
Why this matters

A sign-in that requires a person to remember or transcribe a secret, solve a puzzle, or interpret distorted characters may prevent access. Password managers, paste, and device-based authentication can reduce memory and transcription burdens.
How to apply the criterion

For each authentication step that uses a cognitive function test, provide an alternative without such a test or a mechanism that assists with it, unless an applicable exception applies. The minimum criterion has exceptions for object recognition and identifying personal content. Supporting password managers and paste can be assisting mechanisms; verify that the actual workflow permits them.
Real-world example

A password field blocks paste and password-manager filling. This forces a person to remember and manually transcribe a secret. Allowing paste and compatible autofill can provide assistance with that cognitive task.

<label for="password">Password</label>
<input id="password" type="password" name="password" autocomplete="current-password">

Avoid scripts that intercept and cancel paste. Test the actual sign-in flow, including any second-factor challenge and recovery. The minimum criterion provides exceptions for object recognition and identification of personal content; an alternative or an assisting mechanism may also address the requirement. A single HTML attribute does not by itself prove the complete process is accessible.
Review and testing

Do not assume a one-time code is automatically accessible if the user must memorize and retype it and no assistance is provided. An authentication alternative must remain available throughout the relevant step. Test with a password manager and paste, and examine recovery and multi-factor steps too.
Evaluate every authentication step

A sign-in can appear accessible while account recovery or a second factor blocks paste or demands memorizing a code. Trace the complete path a learner must take, including failed sign-in, recovery and any required second factor. Identify the cognitive task at each step, then check for an alternative or an assisting mechanism that the learner can actually use.

Password-manager support, paste, and device mechanisms are potential assistance, but their effectiveness depends on implementation and user access. The minimum criterion includes specified exceptions for recognizing objects and identifying personal content. It does not follow that every CAPTCHA or photograph challenge is accessible for everyone; test the actual path with intended users.
Authentication is a sequence

A password field is only one part of authentication. A learner may also face a one-time code, an account-recovery challenge, or a second factor. For each step, identify whether the person must remember, manipulate, or transcribe information, and whether a supported alternative or assistance lets them complete that step. Allowing paste and password-manager fill can reduce the burden of a password test.

Test the real flow with the intended browser and devices. A visible paste command is insufficient if the field or application discards pasted text. The minimum criterion includes specific exceptions for object recognition and identification of personal content; those exceptions do not establish that a particular challenge is usable by everyone. Consider recovery and second-factor access rather than evaluating only the first screen.
Walkthrough: mapping a sign-in journey

Trace a learner from account identifier to password, second factor, failed login, and recovery. At each step, list any task involving memory, transcription, or another cognitive function test. Check whether the learner can use an alternative that avoids the test or an assisting mechanism. For a password field, password-manager fill and paste can support a user who cannot reliably memorize or transcribe the value.

Test those mechanisms rather than assuming they work because the browser offers them. Attempt password-manager fill and paste into the actual fields, submit the result, and verify that application code does not block or alter it. Repeat for a one-time code where relevant. Check that the learner can find and operate any alternative without first passing the inaccessible test.

The minimum criterion has specified exceptions for recognizing objects and identifying personal content. Assess the exact challenge and its context; the exceptions do not mean that every visual puzzle is usable by every learner. A complete evaluation includes recovery and required second factors, since an accessible first password screen does not help if a mandatory later step blocks the same learner.
Apply the distinction

For a one-time code, test whether the learner can paste the code or use supported autofill on the actual device. If the UI divides the code into several boxes, verify that a pasted complete code is handled correctly rather than forcing a digit-by-digit transcription. Check the subsequent recovery route too. If an alternative is offered, the learner needs to reach it without first completing the inaccessible test it is intended to replace. The minimum criterion includes specified exceptions for object recognition and personal content; those are separate from the general options of an alternative or assisting mechanism and should not be generalized to every challenge.
Review a second case

Review case: A one-time code arrives by email and the form divides it across six inputs. If a learner pastes the complete code, the application should support a practical assisting mechanism rather than forcing the person to remember and transcribe one digit at a time. Test paste and the device’s available autofill in the real form; inspect whether focus movement, hidden fields, or input validation disrupts the operation. Also test the required recovery path and any second factor. An alternative is not useful if the learner must first solve the inaccessible challenge to reach it. The minimum criterion includes specified exceptions for object recognition and personal content, but their presence does not establish that a visual puzzle is broadly usable.
Implementation and verification

Trace sign-in, required second factors, and recovery, identifying any cognitive function test along the route. Paste and password-manager support can assist with a password, but test that the form actually permits them. Where a step requires remembering or transcribing information, assess the available alternative or assistance and the criterion's stated exceptions. An option available only after sign-in cannot help someone blocked before sign-in. Verify that a learner can reach recovery, complete the necessary steps, and return to the protected task on supported devices.

Follow the learner from the initial instructions through submission, recovery, and final confirmation. Try a realistic mistake, record the message and focus behavior, correct it, and verify the final data. Test the server response as well, because browser validation cannot cover every rejection. Use representative test values that do not expose real personal or financial information in the evidence. Review the experience using keyboard and, where relevant, a screen reader. Keep instructions, validation logic, and help aligned whenever a form or policy changes. Record the route tested and the resulting behavior so the team can reproduce the issue.
Knowledge check
Which can help satisfy the minimum authentication criterion for a password field? Consider the consequences of each approach before continuing.
Required practical activity

Audit a sign-in and its second factor. Identify each memory or transcription demand, then test password-manager fill, paste, or an alternative that removes the demand. Record the barrier, the change you made, and the evidence from your test.
Key takeaway
Assistance can reduce the cognitive burden of remembering or transcribing a password. Consult the complete WCAG 2.2 criterion for its scope and exceptions.
Reference: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/

lessons.title: 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced)
lessons.objective: Apply the enhanced accessible-authentication requirement

content.text: Learning objectives
Apply the enhanced accessible-authentication requirement. This lesson addresses WCAG 2.2 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) (Level AAA).
Why this matters

The enhanced AAA criterion removes the minimum criterion’s exceptions for recognizing objects and identifying personal content. A visual puzzle or selecting a familiar photograph can still be inaccessible to some people, even if it avoids a conventional password.
How to apply the criterion

For each authentication step involving a cognitive function test, provide an alternative that does not require that test or a mechanism that assists the person in completing it. An accessible device-based sign-in or a properly supported password manager may help, depending on the complete flow.
Real-world example

A sign-in asks a user to choose their own photograph as an authentication challenge. That can qualify for an exception at the minimum level, but the enhanced criterion does not retain the exception. Provide an accessible alternative or assistance with the cognitive function test.
<button type="button">Sign in with a passkey</button>

This is an interface illustration rather than a complete passkey implementation. Test whether the chosen method and its enrollment, second-factor, and account-recovery steps are accessible to the intended user. The enhanced criterion removes the object-recognition and personal-content exceptions but retains the possibility of an alternative or assisting mechanism.
Review and testing

Distinguish the enhanced requirement from the minimum requirement: the object-recognition and personal-content exceptions are not available here. Evaluate enrollment, sign-in, second factor, and recovery separately. A biometric method is useful only if the person can use the device and another accessible path is available when needed.
Enhanced authentication and recovery

The enhanced criterion removes the object-recognition and personal-content exceptions that appear at the minimum level. A photograph-selection challenge cannot rely on those exceptions to meet the enhanced requirement. If it uses a cognitive function test, provide an alternative that avoids the test or a mechanism that assists with completing it.

A passkey button is not enough to assess the whole service. Can the learner enroll, use an available device, complete any second factor, and recover an account without an inaccessible cognitive test? Check alternative paths where devices are unavailable and verify that help and instructions are usable. Security mechanisms must actually work; a label describing an option is only the beginning of implementation.
Enhanced authentication across all paths

The enhanced criterion retains the need for an alternative or assisting mechanism where an authentication step uses a cognitive function test, but it does not include the minimum criterion’s object-recognition and personal-content exceptions. A challenge that asks the learner to identify a familiar photograph therefore needs the enhanced criterion’s alternative or assistance if it involves such a test.

Map enrollment, ordinary sign-in, second factor, and recovery as separate paths. A device-based option may reduce memory demands, but verify what happens when the device is unavailable and whether the remaining required steps create a barrier. Test password-manager and paste support where relevant. Do not claim that a single button or a particular technology proves the entire flow meets the criterion.
Walkthrough: checking the enhanced requirement

A service offers password-manager compatible sign-in, but account recovery requires the learner to identify a personal photograph. Evaluate recovery as part of the authentication journey. The enhanced criterion does not include the object-recognition and personal-content exceptions found in the minimum criterion. If that step uses a cognitive function test, an alternative without the test or an assisting mechanism is needed.

List each available route and the assumptions it makes. A passkey can reduce a memory burden when the learner has an enrolled device and can operate it, but the review must also consider the route available when that device is lost. A route advertised as an alternative is ineffective if its setup itself requires completing an inaccessible mandatory challenge.

Exercise enrollment, ordinary sign-in, second factor, and recovery using representative devices. Verify password-manager and paste behavior where applicable and record what actually happens at each step. Do not assume a technology name proves conformance: the result depends on the implementation and the complete set of required authentication steps.
Apply the distinction

A recovery process that asks a user to select their own picture may use personal-content identification, an exception available at the minimum level but absent at the enhanced level. Examine whether it functions as a cognitive test and whether a usable alternative or assisting mechanism is provided. Likewise, a passkey can be a valuable alternative, but check enrollment, device availability, and recovery instead of evaluating only the sign-in button. Test every mandatory factor in sequence. Record which route a learner can actually complete and what assistance it provides; an inaccessible fallback can leave a user locked out even when the ordinary route is well designed.
Review a second case

Review case: A service permits password-manager fill on its normal login screen but requires a personal-photo challenge for recovery. Assess recovery separately: the enhanced criterion does not carry over the minimum criterion’s personal-content and object-recognition exceptions. Where that challenge is a cognitive function test, the learner needs an alternative without the test or an assisting mechanism. Test the alternate path from the point where recovery begins, including any required second factor and enrollment step. A passkey can reduce memorization, but verify the user can access a suitable device and has a usable recovery route if the device is unavailable. Document the complete path and observed assistance rather than declaring conformance based on a single button.
Implementation and verification

Review every required authentication and recovery step against the enhanced criterion, not only the initial form. Object recognition and identifying personal content cannot rely on the exceptions available at the minimum level. If a cognitive function test remains, provide a qualifying alternative or assistance. A passkey helps only if the learner can enroll, use the available device, and recover access when the device is unavailable. Record each route and its dependencies, then test it with relevant assistive technology. Verify the alternative provides real authentication rather than an unprotected bypass.

Follow the learner from the initial instructions through submission, recovery, and final confirmation. Try a realistic mistake, record the message and focus behavior, correct it, and verify the final data. Test the server response as well, because browser validation cannot cover every rejection. Use representative test values that do not expose real personal or financial information in the evidence. Review the experience using keyboard and, where relevant, a screen reader. Keep instructions, validation logic, and help aligned whenever a form or policy changes. Record the route tested and the resulting behavior so the team can reproduce the issue.
Knowledge check
Which exception from the minimum criterion is absent from the enhanced criterion? Consider the consequences of each approach before continuing.
Required practical activity

Compare an image-selection challenge and a passkey or password-manager flow. Identify cognitive tests, available assistance, and any inaccessible step in recovery. Record the barrier, the change you made, and the evidence from your test.
Key takeaway
The enhanced criterion does not include those two exceptions. Consult the complete WCAG 2.2 criterion for its scope and exceptions.
Reference: https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/

elements.title: A Portuguese page is tagged as English. What is the likely effect for speech users?
choices: Speech software may apply the wrong language pronunciation rules.
Speech software will always infer Portuguese from the browser's location.

elements.name: q2
elements.title: A technical article uses a word in a specialized sense. What does a reader need to find?
choices: Only a list of unrelated meanings for the same word.
A definition that explains the intended sense in this article.

elements.name: q3
elements.title: A dense eligibility policy is difficult for its audience to read. Which option can support understanding?
choices: Supplement it with a simpler explanation preserving the eligibility conditions.
Remove all conditions to reduce the total number of words.

elements.name: q4
elements.title: Someone tabs through a page to explore links. Which behavior is predictable?
choices: Each link opens immediately when focus arrives.
The links receive focus without opening their destinations until activated.

elements.name: q5
elements.title: A familiar site header appears across multiple pages. What can help users find its recurring links?
choices: Keep the links in a consistent relative sequence.
Randomize the sequence to highlight different destinations.

elements.name: q6
elements.title: An application opens a new view automatically without a user request. What control can satisfy the relevant AAA criterion?
choices: A notice shown after the new view has already opened.
A mechanism to turn off that automatic change of context.

elements.name: q7
elements.title: A required input is empty after form submission. What information should the error convey?
choices: Which input has the error and what is wrong, in text.
Only that the form contains an error, indicated by color.

elements.name: q8
elements.title: A field rejects a value and a safe correction is known. What should the interface offer?
choices: A repeated error message with no correction guidance.
An actionable suggestion for correcting the value.

elements.name: q9
elements.title: A learner needs help interpreting a specific field. What makes help context-sensitive?
choices: It addresses the information needed for that field and task.
It directs the learner to a generic page unrelated to the field.

elements.name: q10
elements.title: During one process a person must supply information already entered earlier. What can prevent unnecessary repetition?
choices: Require a fresh entry regardless of whether an exception applies.
Make the previously supplied information available for selection or reuse.

choices: Update the root language to match the new predominant content.
Leave the original root language because the URL did not change.

elements.name: q2
elements.title: A German quotation ends and an English explanation follows. Where should the German language attribute end?
choices: After the English explanation so both paragraphs inherit German.
At the end of the German quotation.

elements.name: q3
elements.title: An idiom is confusing to an unfamiliar reader. Which glossary entry addresses the issue?
choices: An explanation of the idiom's intended meaning in that passage.
A list of the individual words without explaining the idiom.

elements.name: q4
elements.title: An abbreviation has different meanings in medicine and computing. Which expansion should a computing lesson offer?
choices: The most common expansion regardless of context.
The expansion that matches its use in the computing lesson.

elements.name: q5
elements.title: A simplified enrollment guide leaves out a required document. How should it be improved?
choices: Add the omitted requirement using clear language.
Keep it omitted because shorter text is always easier to understand.

elements.name: q6
elements.title: An audio pronunciation guide is offered for an ambiguous word. What helps a reader who cannot hear it?
choices: Require the reader to infer the pronunciation from the audio player icon.
Provide a suitable written pronunciation guide as well.

elements.name: q7
elements.title: A validation script puts focus on an error field and the field opens a new page. What should be changed?
choices: Prevent the context change on focus and use an explicit action if navigation is needed.
Move focus to a different field that also opens a page on focus.

elements.name: q8
elements.title: A filter updates a preview in place without moving focus or navigating. What should the reviewer determine?
choices: Treat every visual update as an automatic context change.
Whether the update actually changes context before concluding that this criterion fails.

elements.name: q9
elements.title: A mobile menu adds a page-specific link but retains the shared links' relative order. What does this fact mean?
choices: Adding the link alone does not violate the relative-order requirement.
Any added link automatically violates consistent navigation.

elements.name: q10
elements.title: A catalog search and a help search have different scopes. How should they be named?
choices: Force identical names even when the controls search different resources.
Use names that communicate their distinct functions.

elements.name: q11
elements.title: A learner disables automatic progression. What should the team verify?
choices: The setting prevents the automatic transition when the learner returns.
The setting label changes even if the transition still occurs.

elements.name: q12
elements.title: A learner rearranges their own dashboard and moves the Help link. How does that affect the review?
choices: Treat any user-selected arrangement as automatically prohibited.
Consider the user-initiated change separately from the default order.

elements.name: q13
elements.title: A form summary says “Two errors” without identifying either item. What would improve error identification?
choices: Identify each affected field and describe its error in text.
Replace the summary text with a red triangle.

elements.name: q14
elements.title: Several related radio buttons form one question. What can identify the group?
choices: The placeholder of a separate text field.
A group label such as a fieldset legend alongside the option labels.

elements.name: q15
elements.title: A login error could reveal whether a specific account exists. What should a reviewer consider?
choices: Whether disclosing the suggestion would jeopardize security.
Always reveal the exact account status because every suggestion is mandatory.

elements.name: q16
elements.title: A legal submission relies on reversal as its safeguard. What should be verified?
choices: That the page merely mentions support as a possible future contact.
That the user can actually reverse the submission and learn the outcome.

elements.name: q17
elements.title: Opening field help clears the form. What is an appropriate improvement?
choices: Keep entered values while the user opens and closes accessible help.
Warn users that opening help will erase their answers.

elements.name: q18
elements.title: A review screen lets a user edit a profile before final submission. What must be tested?
choices: The original value is submitted because the review screen appeared.
The corrected value is the one ultimately submitted.

elements.name: q19
elements.title: A billing address is different from shipping. How should reuse work?
choices: Offer the shipping address while allowing an alternative billing address.
Force the shipping address as billing with no edit option.

elements.name: q20
elements.title: An accessible first step is followed by a mandatory memorization test in recovery. What should be assessed?
choices: Only the first step, because recovery is outside the authentication journey.
Whether recovery provides a qualifying alternative or assistance.

elements.name: q21
elements.title: A passkey exists but enrollment requires an inaccessible cognitive test. What should be reviewed?
choices: Whether enrollment and recovery provide a usable qualifying route.
Only whether the passkey button is displayed.
